title: Literature: The Big Picture
objective: After this level you can explain what literature is and trace its path from spoken myths to the modern novel.
summary: Literature is named for letters (Latin littera), yet it began as spoken stories. It runs from myths told aloud to clay tablets, epics like Gilgamesh and Homer, and the novel.

cards.headline: Literature is named after letters. It started without any.
cards.body: The word comes from the Latin littera, a letter of the alphabet. Yet scholars also speak of oral literature: stories and poems passed on by voice, by people who had no writing at all. So how did literature get from spoken stories to the novel on your shelf?

cards.headline: What counts as literature?
cards.body: In its simplest sense, literature is a body of written works. But the word usually means something narrower: imaginative poems and prose, prized for how well they're made. And it isn't only written. A poem kept alive in people's memories counts as oral literature. Your shopping list, sadly, doesn't count, even though it's written down.

cards.headline: From heroes to people
cards.body: Notice what changes along that line. Gilgamesh and Homer's poems are epics: long poems about heroic deeds. The novel, the newest form here, is an invented story in prose, long and complex. Where the epic lifts its heroes up, the novel often shows life as unheroic, imperfect, even absurd. The epic gave you heroes. The novel gave you people.

title: Myth, Legend, Fable and Folk Tale
objective: After this level you can tell a myth from a legend, a fable (like Aesop's) and a folk tale.
summary: A fable is an animal tale with a moral, like Aesop's fox and the "sour grapes". A myth is a sacred traditional story, a legend is told as history, and folk tales change with each teller.

cards.headline: Say "sour grapes" and you're quoting a fox.
cards.body: In an old fable, a fox jumps again and again for a bunch of grapes and misses every time. Finally he walks off, calling them sour grapes, not worth the trouble. That's a fable. It's one of four kinds of traditional story people mix up all the time. Here's how to tell them apart.

cards.fact: A fable teaches a lesson, and usually tells you what it is.
cards.context: Fables usually star animals that talk and act like people, and they poke at human follies. A moral is woven in, often stated at the end. The fox's, in The Aesop for Children (1919): "There are many who pretend to despise and belittle that which is beyond their reach." Most famous fables are credited to Aesop, a likely legendary Greek; the earliest known collection under his name dates to the 4th century BCE.

cards.headline: Told as history, true or not
cards.body: The key to a legend is that it's told as history. William Tell, Switzerland's hero of freedom, is said to have shot an apple off his son's head. The story is tied to a real country and a real struggle, yet there's no evidence Tell ever existed. And a myth isn't a polite word for a lie. Scholars use it for a traditional sacred story. In this tree, myth never means false.

title: Gilgamesh, the Oldest Epic
objective: After this level you can retell the Epic of Gilgamesh and explain its king's failed search for a way to escape death.
summary: Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, loses his friend Enkidu and seeks Utnapishtim to escape death. He wins a plant of youth, a serpent takes it, and he goes home mortal.

cards.headline: Often called the earliest great story, it's about a king who can't face death.
cards.body: The Epic of Gilgamesh is often cited as the earliest significant work of literature to survive. Its hero is Gilgamesh, king of Uruk in Mesopotamia. He can beat monsters. What he can't beat is the one thing every reader shares with him.

cards.headline: A real king and a wild friend
cards.body: There probably was a real Gilgamesh: he likely ruled Uruk in the first half of the 3rd millennium BCE. In the epic, the gods create Enkidu, a wild man who lives among animals, to restrain him. The two test their strength against each other and become close friends. Together they kill Humbaba, guardian of a remote cedar forest, and the Bull of Heaven. So far, a buddy adventure.

cards.headline: Then his friend dies
cards.body: The gods decide Enkidu must die for killing the bull, and his death hits Gilgamesh hard. Now death is personal. So the king makes a dangerous journey to find Utnapishtim, the one man who survived the great flood, to learn from him how to escape death.

mascot.line: Hold on to Utnapishtim, the flood survivor. His flood is the star of the next level.

cards.fact: A snake ate his second chance.
cards.context: Utnapishtim tells Gilgamesh where to find a plant that renews youth. He gets it. Then a serpent seizes it, and Gilgamesh goes home to Uruk still mortal. The fullest text of his story survives on 12 broken clay tablets in Akkadian, found at Nineveh in the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal. Writing, pressed into clay, carried a king's fear of death for thousands of years.

title: A Flood Story on a Clay Tablet
objective: After this level you can explain how the flood story in Gilgamesh was recognized in 1872 and how it parallels the flood in Genesis.
summary: In 1872 George Smith read a flood story on the 11th tablet of Gilgamesh. Like Noah, Utnapishtim builds a boat, saves animals and sends out birds, but the reasons and endings differ.

cards.headline: In 1872, a man read a broken clay tablet and started to undress.
cards.body: According to a later account, George Smith of the British Museum jumped up and rushed about the room in great excitement, then began taking off his clothes. What could an old tablet say to do that to a person?

cards.headline: A ship, a mountain, a dove
cards.body: Smith had been apprenticed to a banknote engraver at 14, then taught himself to read cuneiform. On one tablet, as he later wrote, his eye caught a ship resting on a mountain, then a dove sent out that found no resting place and came back. It sounded like Noah's flood in Genesis. It was on the 11th tablet of the 12-tablet Epic of Gilgamesh.

cards.headline: Same shape, different meaning
cards.body: Scholars see Babylonian flood traditions as the source of features of the biblical story, such as building and stocking the ark and the waters going down. But the two tell different stories. In the Babylonian flood, the gods disagree; in Genesis, the flood answers human wrongdoing. And the endings split: Utnapishtim joins the immortal gods, while Noah's family is sent to start history again.

cards.context: Smith presented his find to the Society of Biblical Archaeology in 1872, with Prime Minister Gladstone in the audience. The Daily Telegraph then paid for an expedition to Nineveh. In May 1873, digging there, Smith found a fragment he believed completed the flood account.

title: How the World Began
objective: After this level you can compare three common shapes of creation story: order out of chaos, the cosmic egg and the earth diver.
summary: Creation myths tell how the world began. Babylon and Greece start from chaos, Chinese tellings from a cosmic egg, and the Haudenosaunee from earth a muskrat brings up from the water.

cards.headline: Before there was anything, what was there?
cards.body: Creation myths answer it. A creation myth is a symbolic story of how the world began and how people first came to live in it. Told across oceans and centuries, many of them follow a few familiar shapes. Here are three.

cards.headline: Shape 1: order out of chaos
cards.body: In Babylon's Enuma Elish, the universe starts as watery chaos with no sky or land, where the sea goddess Tiamat and the sweet-water god Apsu mingle their waters. The god Marduk defeats Tiamat and cuts her in two: one half becomes the earth, the other the heavens. Babylonians recited it at Akitu, their New Year festival. Greece starts in the same place. Hesiod's Theogony, in Hugh G. Evelyn-White's translation: "Verily at the first Chaos came to be."

cards.headline: Shape 2: the cosmic egg
cards.body: A world born from a cosmic egg is a widespread idea. In Chinese tellings, Pan Gu came out of chaos, an egg, and pushed heaven and earth apart. Another version builds the world from his body: his eyes became the sun and moon, his blood the rivers. These tellings date from the 3rd to the 6th century. The universe as a very big breakfast.

cards.headline: Shape 3: the earth diver
cards.body: Earth-diver myths are widespread too. The Haudenosaunee tell of Sky Woman, who fell from the Sky World toward endless water. Birds caught her and set her on the back of a great turtle. Animal after animal dove for earth. The muskrat came up with a little earth in his claws, and on the turtle's back it grew into North America: Turtle Island.

title: Homer: Poems Made to Be Sung
objective: After this level you can explain how oral poets composed epics like Homer's from stock phrases and repeated scenes.
summary: Homeric singers composed aloud with formulas, stock phrases like "rosy-fingered Dawn" that fit the meter, and type-scenes like feasts and arming. Parry heard the method alive in the 1930s.

cards.headline: In the Odyssey, the sun keeps rising in exactly the same words.
cards.body: In Samuel Butler's translation, "the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn" appears again and again. A lazy poet? No. It's a clue to how the poems were made. Homer's epics grew out of a centuries-old tradition of singers who composed out loud.

cards.headline: Phrases cut to fit
cards.body: Homer's poems run in a strict meter, the dactylic hexameter. Oral poets kept ready-made phrases, called formulas, refined over generations to fit that meter. "Rosy-fingered dawn" and "wine-dark sea" each fit a set place in the line. Need a sunrise? The phrase is waiting. With enough formulas, a singer could keep a long poem flowing without stopping to hunt for words.
cards.callout: A formula is a phrase shaped to fit the rhythm.

cards.headline: Scenes on repeat
cards.body: Singers inherited whole scenes too. Scholars call them type-scenes: recurring blocks of story with a set structure, like a sacrifice, welcoming a guest, launching a ship or a warrior putting on armor. Homer's tradition handed down phrases, scenes and plots, and each singer reshaped them in performance. Learn the pattern for a feast once, and you can serve up a feast anywhere.

mascot.line: This is the key move: memory plus building blocks can hold a whole epic. Watch for memory again in Level 9.

cards.fact: A singer who could not read performed about 12,000 lines.
cards.context: In the 1930s, Milman Parry transcribed that epic from a singer in Yugoslavia. With his student Albert Lord, Parry recorded oral poets composing as they performed: the method alive, with no page in sight. Many scholars think writing, through dictation or later editing, then turned Homer's fluid performances into the fixed texts we read.

title: Ovid's Metamorphoses
objective: After this level you can explain why Ovid's poem of transformations became the myth book later writers borrowed from.
summary: Ovid's Metamorphoses (about 8 CE) strings myths of transformation from creation to Julius Caesar. Its Daphne and Pyramus and Thisbe fed poets and painters for centuries, Shakespeare included.

cards.headline: A woman becomes a tree to escape a god. Ovid made sure we'd all hear of it.
cards.body: Daphne refused every suitor, Apollo included. When the god chased her, she prayed for rescue and became a laurel tree. Apollo claimed the laurel for poets and, in Rome, for triumphs. Her story is one of many in a single Roman poem.

cards.headline: A poem made of changes
cards.body: Ovid finished the Metamorphoses, 15 books of Latin hexameter verse, about 8 CE. It collects myths, many from Greek sources, and in each a transformation plays a part. They run in order from the creation of the world (chaos turned to order, the first change of all) to the death and deification of Julius Caesar. That same year, the emperor banished Ovid to Tomis.

cards.headline: Lovers, a wall and a mulberry
cards.body: Pyramus and Thisbe are Babylonian lovers forbidden to marry, who whisper through a crack in the wall between their houses. They plan to meet at a mulberry tree. Thisbe flees a lioness and drops her veil; Pyramus finds it, thinks she is dead and kills himself, and Thisbe follows. The transformation? The tree's snow-white berries are dyed dark purple by his blood.

cards.fact: For centuries, writers and painters borrowed from Ovid.
cards.context: Ovid gave scores of Greek legends the form later generations knew. From the 15th to the 17th centuries, it's hard to name a poet or painter of note who didn't owe him something. In Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, workmen act a farcical Pyramus and Thisbe, and the same tale was one inspiration for Romeo and Juliet.

title: Hou Yi, Chang'e and the Moon
objective: After this level you can retell the Chinese myth of the archer who shot down nine suns and the woman who flew to the Moon.
summary: In Chinese myth the archer Hou Yi shot down nine of ten burning suns. His wife Chang'e swallowed his elixir of immortality and fled to the Moon, honored at the Mid-Autumn Festival.

cards.headline: Ten suns in the sky at once, and the earth began to burn.
cards.body: In Chinese myth, ten suns were burning up the earth. The job of saving it fell to one man with a bow.

cards.headline: Nine arrows
cards.body: He was Hou Yi, the Lord Archer, whose skill with a bow earned him undying fame. He shot down 9 of the 10 suns, leaving the one we still have. Even here, tellings differ: one account says he shot 8 of 9. Myths don't come with one official edition.

cards.headline: The stolen elixir
cards.body: Hou Yi received an elixir of immortality from a great goddess, the Queen Mother of the West. Before he could take it, his wife Chang'e swallowed it herself and became immortal. Fearing his anger, she fled to the Moon, where she lives in the Palace of Boundless Cold. In paintings, a white rabbit beside her pounds the elixir with a mortar and pestle.

cards.fact: Look for Chang'e at the Mid-Autumn Festival.
cards.context: On the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, people celebrate Chang'e with the Mid-Autumn Festival and eat mooncakes, rich pastries with sweet or savory fillings. Some look for the outline of a toad on the Moon, because in one legend Chang'e became a toad. Her story isn't only in old books. It comes around every autumn.

title: Amaterasu and Japan's Kojiki
objective: After this level you can retell the story of the sun goddess who hid in a cave, from Japan's oldest surviving book.
summary: Japan's Kojiki (712) was written down from Hieda no Are's memory. In it, the sun goddess Amaterasu hides in a cave, and the gods lure her out with a mirror, a dance and laughter.

cards.headline: The sun goddess hid in a cave, and the whole world went dark.
cards.body: Amaterasu is the sun goddess of Shinto. This story of her comes from the Kojiki, the oldest surviving book from Japan. To get the sun back, the gods didn't use force. They threw a party.

cards.headline: A book from memory
cards.body: The Kojiki (Record of Ancient Matters) began in someone's head. Emperor Temmu had a court attendant, Hieda no Are, memorize Japan's earliest myths and records. Then the courtier Ō no Yasumaro wrote them down, using Chinese characters, and presented the book to the empress in 712. Much of Shinto thought is based on interpretations of its myths.

cards.headline: A storm god behaving badly
cards.body: Amaterasu's brother Susanoo, the storm god, went on a rampage. He broke down the divisions in her rice fields, defiled her home and threw a flayed horse into her weaving hall. Amaterasu withdrew into a cave in protest, and darkness fell upon the world. No sun, no day.

cards.headline: Laughter opens the cave
cards.body: The gods hung a mirror and jewels on a sakaki tree outside the cave. The goddess Amenouzume danced, the gods laughed loudly, and Amaterasu was drawn out. Quickly, they threw a shimenawa, a sacred rope of rice straw, across the entrance so she couldn't hide again. The imperial family claims descent from her, and at the Grand Shrine of Ise she is present in a mirror, one of the three Imperial Treasures.

cards.headline: A fallen city kept the king's library
cards.body: The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal had his scribes collect and copy ancient texts of every kind, from prayers to fables and epics. In 612 BCE an alliance including Babylonians and Medes sacked his capital, Nineveh, and the ruined walls buried the clay tablets. From 1845, Austen Henry Layard and then Hormuzd Rassam dug them out, and more than 20,000 tablets and fragments went to the British Museum. Among them: the 12 tablets of Gilgamesh.

title: Odin, Thor and Loki
objective: After this level you can describe the main Norse gods and the two Eddas from Iceland that preserved their stories.
summary: Odin traded an eye for wisdom, Thor's hammer returns like a boomerang, and Loki shape-shifts. Their stories survive in two Icelandic books, the Poetic Edda and Snorri's Prose Edda.

cards.headline: You say a Norse god's name every week.
cards.body: Thursday is Thor's day: the Romans' dies Jovis, Jove's day, became Thor's day. Thor was a god of all the early Germanic peoples, and his name was their word for thunder. Our fullest source for his stories, and for the other Norse gods, is two books from Iceland. Meet the gods first, then the books.

cards.headline: Odin traded an eye for wisdom
cards.body: Odin is one of the principal Norse gods. From earliest times he was a war god and the protector of heroes, and fallen warriors joined him in Valhalla, his hall in Asgard. He was also the god of poets and the great magician among the gods. And he has only one eye: he gave the other in exchange for wisdom. For Odin, knowing things was worth the price of an eye.

cards.headline: The strongman and the shape-shifter
cards.body: Thor is a red-bearded warrior of enormous strength, an enemy of giants but kind to humans. His hammer, Mjollnir, comes back when he throws it, like a boomerang. Loki is a different sort: a cunning trickster who can change his shape and even his sex. His father was a giant, yet he counts among the gods as a companion of Odin and Thor. He is also the main cause of the god Balder's death, and as punishment he is bound to a rock.

mascot.line: People mix up the two Eddas. The Poetic Edda is the old poems; the Prose Edda is Snorri's guide to them.

cards.headline: Two Eddas: a book of poems and a poets' handbook
cards.body: The Poetic Edda gathers mythological and heroic poems composed between 800 and 1100, in a manuscript from the second half of the 13th century. The Prose Edda was written about 1220 by Snorri Sturluson, an Icelandic poet, historian and chieftain. It's a textbook to teach young poets the old meters and the myths their poems allude to. So one of the best guides to the Norse gods is a manual for poets.

title: Ragnarök, the Twilight of the Gods
objective: After this level you can retell the Norse story of the end of the world and its rebirth.
summary: Ragnarok, the Norse end of the world: a three-year winter, monsters loose, Odin swallowed by Fenrir, Thor killed by the serpent's poison, then the earth rises again with two humans.

cards.headline: The Norse gods know how their world ends. They lose.
cards.body: Ragnarok is the end of the world of gods and men. It's told in the Voluspa, a 10th-century Icelandic poem, and retold in Snorri's 13th-century Prose Edda. Odin, Thor and Loki all have parts to play in the last act. Not all of them make it to the curtain call.

cards.headline: First, a winter that won't end
cards.body: It begins with the Fimbulwinter, the "Mighty Winter", which lasts three years. Then the monsters get loose. The great wolf Fenrir and Jormungand, the Midgard serpent, are freed. Remember Loki, bound to a rock? He escapes too, and steers Naglfar, a ship made of the nails of dead men. Norse myth does not do cozy.

cards.headline: The gods fall
cards.body: In the last battle, Fenrir swallows Odin. Thor kills the serpent, but its poison kills him. Surtr, the fire giant, leads the sons of Muspelheim across Bifrost and shatters the rainbow bridge. The sun turns black and the earth sinks into the sea. By now, it looks like the end of everything.

cards.fact: Then the earth rises again.
cards.context: It comes back up out of the sea, and a woman and a man, Lif and Lifthrasir, come out of the world-tree. Some gods survive to make a new home, and Balder, the god whose death Loki caused, comes back from the dead to join them. So the Norse end of the world isn't the end of the story. It's the start of the next one.

title: The Icelandic Sagas
objective: After this level you can explain what the sagas of Icelanders are and why their plain, realistic prose stands out in medieval writing.
summary: The sagas of Icelanders, prose stories written down in the 13th century about farming families of 930 to 1030, stand out for their realism and objective style, as in Njals saga.

cards.headline: Iceland's greatest medieval stories star farmers.
cards.body: Iceland's kings' sagas have aristocratic heroes who lead armies. The sagas of Icelanders don't: their characters are essentially farmers or farmers' sons. Their authors tried to show Iceland as they knew it, or as they imagined it had been. So what makes these stories stand out?

cards.headline: A saga is a story in prose
cards.body: In medieval Icelandic, a saga is any kind of story or history in prose. The sagas of Icelanders tell of the families who lived in Iceland from 930 to 1030. They were written down in Iceland, mainly in the 13th century, and nothing is known of who wrote them. No author's name, no dedication, just the story.

cards.headline: Told as if it really happened
cards.body: What makes the sagas stand out is how they tell it. They're known for realism, an objective style, tragic dignity and sharp character portraits. The authors aimed to be true to Iceland's land, society and culture, down to the farms and the neighbors. The effect: you read it as if it all really happened.

cards.fact: In Njals saga, a wise farmer's enemies burn his house.
cards.context: Njals saga is often called the greatest of the sagas. Its hero, Njal, is an influential farmer and sage who spends his life in a hopeless struggle, until his enemies burn his house with his family inside. And the language has held still: Icelanders today can read these sagas without difficulty. Imagine reading a 13th-century English story without a dictionary.

title: The Mahabharata
objective: After this level you can describe the Mahabharata's war between two sets of cousins and the Bhagavad Gita spoken on its battlefield.
summary: The Mahabharata tells of the Kaurava and Pandava cousins, a dice game, exile and war; on the brink of battle, Krishna counsels Arjuna in the Bhagavad Gita.

cards.headline: One poem, seven times the Iliad and Odyssey put together.
cards.body: The Mahabharata has almost 100,000 couplets. Tradition credits it to the sage Vyasa, but it grew over centuries and reached its present form about 400 CE. At its heart is a family quarrel that turns into a war.

cards.headline: Cousins, a dice game and exile
cards.body: The quarrel is between two sets of cousins: the Kauravas, sons of Dhritarashtra, and the Pandavas, sons of Pandu. Both want to rule. In a dice game set up by the Kaurava prince Duryodhana, the Pandavas lose their kingdom and are sent into the forest for 12 years. Lesson one of the Mahabharata: never bet the kingdom.

cards.headline: War at Kurukshetra
cards.body: The quarrel ends in a war at Kurukshetra, and every one of the Kauravas is killed. The story never stopped being told: the Mahabharata has been retold in Sanskrit and in local languages, in writing and out loud, throughout South and Southeast Asia.

mascot.line: Keep this: the Bhagavad Gita is a conversation inside the Mahabharata's story, spoken in a chariot before the war.

cards.headline: A conversation before the battle
cards.body: On the brink of battle, Prince Arjuna is overwhelmed with misgivings: across the field are friends and relatives he would have to kill. His charioteer is Krishna, an avatar of the god Vishnu, and their dialogue is the Bhagavad Gita, part of the epic's sixth book. Krishna counsels him on his duty. Many Hindus have long cherished the Gita for spiritual guidance.

title: The Ramayana
objective: After this level you can retell the Ramayana of Rama, Sita and Hanuman and explain how it spread across South and Southeast Asia.
summary: Valmiki's Ramayana: Rama is exiled, Ravana carries off Sita, and Hanuman helps rescue her. The story spread across Southeast Asia, from Thailand's Ramakien to Java's temples.

cards.headline: A prince loses his throne and his wife. A monkey helps him win.
cards.body: That's the Ramayana, the Sanskrit epic of the poet Valmiki: about 24,000 couplets in seven books. And it didn't stay at home. First the story, then where it went.

cards.headline: Fourteen years in the forest
cards.body: Rama is heir to the throne of Ayodhya, but he is sent into exile for 14 years, with his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana. Rama embodies dharma (duty, honor and loyalty): the ideal son, husband and, in the end, king. Then, in the forest, Ravana, the 10-headed demon king of Lanka, carries Sita off.

cards.headline: Hanuman to the rescue
cards.body: With the help of Hanuman, a devoted monkey general, Rama defeats Ravana and rescues Sita: a classic tale of good triumphing over evil. In India the story is still acted out. Ramlila ("Rama's play") stages it during the nine-day festival of Navratri, and Diwali marks Rama's return home from exile.

cards.headline: The story that traveled
cards.body: The Ramayana spread in many forms through Southeast Asia, especially to Cambodia, Indonesia and Thailand. Thailand's version is the Ramakien, and khon, Thailand's traditional dance-drama, is based on it. Scenes from the Ramayana are carved on Indonesian monuments, such as Panataran in eastern Java. One epic, many accents.

title: Sundiata, the Epic of Mali
objective: After this level you can retell the epic of Mali's founder and explain how griots have kept it alive by performance.
summary: Sundiata Keita founded Mali in the 13th century. In the epic, the boy who could not walk stands up on an iron bar and defeats Sumanguru at Kirina. Griots, many with the kora, keep it alive.

cards.headline: Mali's founder was a boy who couldn't walk.
cards.body: Sundiata Keita, who died in 1255, founded the Mali Empire in West Africa. We know his life from oral traditions repeated by griots, West Africa's storytellers. Here's the story they tell, and then the storytellers themselves.

cards.headline: The boy who stood up
cards.body: In the epic, Sogolon's son can't walk as a child, and he and his mother are mocked at court. Then, in one great effort, he pulls himself to his feet on a huge iron bar, and the bar bends into the shape of a bow. The boy everyone laughed at is standing, and the bar isn't.

cards.headline: Exile and return
cards.body: Here the epic meets history. Sumanguru, ruler of a neighboring state, overran Sundiata's homeland and killed his brothers, sparing him because he was a sickly boy. Sundiata went into exile, then came back and defeated Sumanguru decisively at the Battle of Kirina, about 1235.

mascot.line: This connects to Level 6: like Homer's singers, griots carry an epic by voice, not by page.

cards.headline: The griot's kora
cards.body: Griots, called jeli in the Mande languages, are hereditary troubadour-historians. They preserve genealogies, histories and oral traditions, and many play the kora, a long-necked harp lute with 21 strings. In 1960 Djibril Tamsir Niane published a French retelling of the epic, presented as told by the griot Djeli Mamadou Kouyate. Even on paper, a griot does the talking.

title: Anansi and the Tricksters
objective: After this level you can explain what a trickster is, from Anansi the spider to Coyote and Br'er Rabbit.
summary: A trickster is a hero of opposites who wins by guile: Ananse the Akan spider, Coyote and Raven in Native North America, and Br'er Rabbit, from African folklore via enslaved Africans.

cards.headline: To win all the stories, a spider had to catch a big cat.
cards.body: In one Akan story, Ananse asks the sky god Nyame to make him King of All Wisdom Narratives. The price is three impossible tasks: capture a fierce big cat, the hornets and a fairy. Ananse manages all three by cunning, not force. That makes him a trickster.

cards.headline: What makes a trickster
cards.body: A trickster is a story's hero, often an animal with human ways and magical powers, and a bundle of opposites: a creator and a fool, a destroyer and a childish prankster. Tricksters get by on knavery, stupidity, gluttony or guile, and most often a mix of them. Brilliant on Monday, ridiculous on Tuesday.

cards.headline: Ananse, Coyote and Raven
cards.body: Ananse, usually a spider, belongs to the Akan peoples, especially the Asante, and is famous across Africa, the Caribbean and beyond. He teaches values by leading people to the truth through puzzles, example and unexpected twists. In North America, Coyote is possibly the most widely known Native trickster, and Raven plays the part among Northwest Coast peoples.

cards.headline: Br'er Rabbit: small, weak and too clever
cards.body: Br'er Rabbit comes from African folklore, brought to the Americas by enslaved Africans. He keeps outsmarting bigger animals like Br'er Fox and Br'er Bear. Joel Chandler Harris, a white Atlanta journalist, heard the tales from enslaved people on a Georgia plantation and published them from 1880, told by Uncle Remus to a plantation owner's son. The writer Alice Walker protested that Harris had turned her heritage into a white man's publishing commodity.

title: The Popol Vuh
objective: After this level you can retell the K'iche' Maya story in which the gods try mud and wood before making people from maize.
summary: The K'iche' Maya's Popol Vuh, written 1554 to 1558 in the Latin alphabet, tells how the gods made people of mud, then wood, then maize. Ximenez's copy survives in Chicago.

cards.headline: The gods got people right on the third try.
cards.body: The K'iche' Maya of Guatemala tell how the gods first tried mud, then wood, and finally maize. The story is in their Popol Vuh. First, how the book reached us. Then, what went wrong with the first two tries.

cards.headline: A book that nearly vanished
cards.body: The Popol Vuh, roughly "Council Book", was written by the K'iche' Maya between 1554 and 1558, in their own language but in the Latin alphabet. That original is lost. The priest Francisco Ximenez found it in the early 1700s and copied it, and his copy is now in the Newberry Library in Chicago. A Maya book survives thanks to one Spanish priest's handwriting.

cards.headline: Mud, then wood
cards.body: The gods want beings who will praise and remember them. The first, of mud, won't hold its shape and speaks nonsense, so they dissolve it. Next come people of wood. They have no hearts and don't remember their makers. The gods send a great flood, and the wooden people who flee into the forest become monkeys.

cards.fact: At last, people made of maize.
cards.context: The gods finally succeed, making humans from maize. These people see and know so much that the gods fear they'll become as great as gods. So they cloud human sight, like breath on a mirror. Corn isn't just food in this story. It's what people are made of.

title: Why Myths Rhyme
objective: After this level you can explain the main theories for why myths from distant places share patterns: shared roots, contact and shared human minds.
summary: Why myths far apart rhyme: shared roots (Dyaus, Zeus and Jupiter share a name), contact (floods, the Ramayana, Br'er Rabbit travel) and shared minds (Bastian's elementary ideas).

cards.headline: India, Greece and Rome each had a sky god with the same old name.
cards.body: India's Vedic sky god Dyaus, Greece's Zeus and Rome's Jupiter ("Father Jove") have names that go back to one ancestor. Myths from far-apart places keep rhyming like this. Here are three explanations for why.

cards.headline: Explanation one: shared roots
cards.body: The names Dyaus, Zeus and Jupiter are cognates: all three go back to the name of a Proto-Indo-European sky god. India, Greece and Rome inherited him, the way cousins can inherit their grandmother's nose. When myths rhyme because of a common origin, they aren't copies of each other. They're relatives.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. Shared roots means inherited from a common ancestor; contact means borrowed from a neighbor.

cards.headline: Explanation two: contact
cards.body: Stories travel with their tellers. Scholars see Babylonian flood traditions as the source of features of the flood in Genesis (Level 4). The Ramayana spread through Southeast Asia (Level 15), and Br'er Rabbit reached the Americas with enslaved Africans (Level 17). Here the rhyme comes from borrowing.

cards.headline: Explanation three: shared minds
cards.body: The ethnologist Adolf Bastian argued for a psychic unity of humankind: all peoples share certain elementary ideas, which take different forms in different environments. Carl Jung's idea of a collective unconscious is believed to derive from Bastian's theory. On this view, a widespread pattern like the earth diver (Level 5) could arise again and again, with no contact needed.

title: The Shape of a Plot
objective: After this level you can identify exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution in a story.
summary: Freytag (1863) drew drama as a pyramid of five parts. Today: exposition, rising action, climax (the turning point), falling action and resolution, the denouement.

cards.headline: In 1863, a German writer drew the shape of a drama as a pyramid.
cards.body: Gustav Freytag published his answer to how plays are built in Die Technik des Dramas, in Leipzig, in 1863. His picture was simple: tension climbs to a peak, then comes down. Once you see the shape, you start spotting it.

cards.headline: Up the slope, over the top
cards.body: Freytag split a drama into five parts: the introduction, the rise, the climax, the return or fall, and the catastrophe. The climax, from a Greek word for "ladder", is the turning point where rising action turns into falling action. Why "catastrophe" at the end? In tragedy, the ending is often called that. The top of the ladder is where everything tips.

mascot.line: Remember the shape more than the labels: a climb, a peak, a way down, a knot untied.

cards.headline: The five parts, in today's words
cards.body: Today the parts usually go by these names. Exposition introduces the setting, characters and background. Rising action piles on complications that raise the tension. The climax is the peak. Falling action shows the consequences. The resolution, or denouement, ends it. Denouement is French for "unknotting": the complications are unraveled and the conflict is resolved.

cards.fact: Try it on Gilgamesh.
cards.context: Level 3's king makes a good test. Enkidu's death hits him hard and sends him on a dangerous journey to Utnapishtim, to learn how to escape death: rising action. He gets a plant that renews youth, and a serpent seizes it: the turn. He goes home to Uruk still mortal. That quiet homecoming is the resolution.

title: Conflict Drives the Story
objective: After this level you can name the main kinds of conflict and spot which one drives a story.
summary: Conflict is a struggle between opposing forces. External: person vs person, nature or society. Internal: person vs self. Ask what the hero wants and what blocks it.

cards.headline: No trouble, no story.
cards.body: Picture a tale where someone wants something and simply gets it. The end. You wouldn't turn the page. What keeps a story moving is a struggle between two forces, and writers have a name for it: conflict.

cards.headline: Outside or inside
cards.body: A conflict is a struggle between two opposing forces, usually the main character and something else, and it drives the story forward. The other force can be outside: another person, nature or society. That's an external conflict. Or it can be inside the character's own mind. That's an internal conflict, and it can be the hardest fight of all.

cards.headline: Four classic kinds
cards.body: Person vs person: two characters with opposing goals. Person vs nature: a fight with natural forces, like a storm at sea. Person vs society: one character against a society's rules or traditions. Person vs self: a moral struggle inside one mind. Some lists add fate, the supernatural and technology. The opponent changes; the push and pull doesn't.

cards.headline: Ask two questions
cards.body: To find the conflict that drives a story, ask what the main character wants and what stands in the way. Conflict is whatever puts obstacles between a character and that goal. Level 3's Gilgamesh first meets Enkidu in a trial of strength: person against person. Later he wants to escape death, and his journey to Utnapishtim can't get him there.

title: Round and Flat Characters
objective: After this level you can tell round characters from flat ones and trace a character arc.
summary: Forster (1927): flat characters are built round one idea; round ones can surprise convincingly. A dynamic character changes (an arc), like Scrooge.

cards.headline: A novelist sorted every character into two kinds: flat and round.
cards.body: In the spring of 1927, E. M. Forster gave a series of lectures at Trinity College, Cambridge, published that year as Aspects of the Novel. One pair of words from them is this level's tool.

cards.headline: Flat: one idea, one sentence
cards.body: Forster wrote that flat characters, in their purest form, are "constructed round a single idea or quality." You can sum one up in a sentence. His example is Mrs. Micawber in Dickens's David Copperfield: "I never will desert Mr. Micawber." Flat isn't an insult. Forster said flat characters are easily recognized and easily remembered.

cards.headline: Round: the surprise test
cards.body: Round characters are complex and they develop. Forster's test: "The test of a round character is whether it is capable of surprising in a convincing way." A character who never surprises you is flat. One who surprises you but doesn't convince you is a flat character pretending to be round.

cards.headline: The arc: how a character changes
cards.body: A dynamic character goes through major inner change over a story; that path of change is the character's arc. A static character barely changes. What moves them? The story's conflicts and plot. Dickens's A Christmas Carol (1843) is the classic case: a miserly old man, Scrooge, is visited by a series of ghosts and transformed into a kind benefactor.

title: Who Is Telling the Story?
objective: After this level you can identify first person, third person limited and omniscient narration and what each lets a reader know.
summary: Point of view is the story's vantage point. First person: one "I" inside it. Third limited: one character's mind. Omniscient: a panoramic view of many.

cards.headline: The same events can be a shock or a secret, depending on who tells them.
cards.body: Picture a surprise party. Told by the guest of honor, it's a shock at the door. Told by the friend who planned it, it's a secret kept for weeks. Same party. What changes is the vantage point from which the story is presented, which critics call point of view.

cards.headline: First person: "I was there"
cards.body: In first-person narration, the narrator says "I" and is usually a character in the story. You get that narrator's thoughts and feelings, and no one else's. If the narrator didn't see it, or doesn't understand it, neither do you. It's intimate, and it's a keyhole.

cards.headline: Over one shoulder, or everywhere at once
cards.body: Third person limited tells the story from the standpoint of one character, who is not all-knowing: you get that character's thoughts and actions only. Omniscient narration gives a panoramic view of the actions and inner feelings of the characters, and can move freely in time and place. One is a shoulder to look over; the other is a view from the sky.

cards.fact: Forster ranked it right after character.
cards.context: In Aspects of the Novel, once he had sorted flat characters from round, Forster turned to his second device: "the point of view from which the story may be told." Choosing a narrator means choosing what the reader is allowed to know.

title: Can You Trust the Narrator?
objective: After this level you can spot the clues that a narrator is unreliable.
summary: An unreliable narrator lies, leaves out or twists facts, or misreads events (Booth, 1961). Poe's Tell-Tale Heart narrator proves his sanity with proof of the opposite.

cards.headline: A narrator asks, "why will you say that I am mad?" Then he shows you.
cards.body: That question opens Edgar Allan Poe's "The Tell-Tale Heart", published in The Pioneer in 1843. The man telling it insists he is perfectly sane. The story he tells says otherwise.

cards.headline: A narrator who bends the truth
cards.body: An unreliable narrator tells lies, leaves out or twists important information, or presents a skewed reading of events as plain truth. The critic Wayne C. Booth named the idea in his 1961 book The Rhetoric of Fiction. Some narrators are unreliable without meaning to be, through youth or inexperience. Others have motives to mislead.

cards.headline: Clue 1: the proof proves the opposite
cards.body: Poe's narrator offers this as evidence of a sound mind: "I heard all things in the heaven and in the earth. I heard many things in hell. How, then, am I mad?" He also admits the old man he lives with "had never wronged me." He decides to take his life anyway. When the reasons don't add up, the teller is the mystery.

mascot.line: Keep this: read past what the narrator says to what the story shows. When the two don't match, trust the story.

cards.headline: Clue 2: the facts catch up
cards.body: Unreliability shows as you learn more and the new information contradicts what the narrator told you. Poe's narrator is maddened by what he believes is the old man's loud heartbeat. After the murder he believes he can still hear it, and he hysterically confesses. So much for the calm storyteller of the first lines.

title: Theme: What a Story Means
objective: After this level you can tell a story's subject from its theme and state a theme in one sentence.
summary: A theme is a story's central idea: the subject (a word) plus an assertion, in one sentence. A moral tells you how to live; a theme can just reveal.

cards.headline: A fable hands you its meaning. Other stories make you find it.
cards.body: Level 2's fox fable ends with its lesson spelled out: "There are many who pretend to despise and belittle that which is beyond their reach." Other stories leave the meaning for you to find. That meaning is called the theme.

cards.headline: Subject: a word. Theme: a sentence.
cards.body: A theme is the main or central idea of a literary work, its controlling insight. It is not a summary of the characters or events. A handy method: take the topic, which can be a single word like "death", and add an assertion about it. Then write the theme as one sentence, with a subject and a verb.

cards.headline: Try it on Gilgamesh
cards.body: Subject: death. Britannica sees Gilgamesh's quest, which begins after Enkidu dies, as reflecting the human struggle to come to terms with death. And though he fails to win immortality, the epic suggests his legacy as a ruler and builder will endure. One theme sentence: even a king can't escape death, but what he builds can outlast him.

cards.headline: A theme isn't always a moral
cards.body: A moral is a recommendation for how to live. A theme doesn't have to be one. So when you look for a theme, ask what the story reveals, not what it teaches. A story can show you a hard problem and leave you holding it.

title: Symbols and Motifs
objective: After this level you can explain how an object can stand for an idea and how a repeated motif builds meaning.
summary: A symbol stands for something bigger: Noah's dove, Ozymandias's broken statue. A motif recurs through a work and points to its theme, like Poe's heartbeat.

cards.headline: A bird with a leaf in its beak told Noah the flood was over.
cards.body: In the King James Bible, the dove comes back to the ark, "and, lo, in her mouth was an olive leaf pluckt off: so Noah knew that the waters were abated from off the earth." A bird and a leaf, carrying a message far bigger than themselves.

cards.headline: One thing standing for another
cards.body: A symbol is one thing, usually a physical object, used to stand for something more abstract. It works by association or convention: the lion is a symbol of courage. And the dove? Today it's the bird portrayed and called the "dove of peace". An object you can hold, pointing at an idea you can't.

cards.headline: A broken statue that stands for fallen power
cards.body: In Shelley's sonnet "Ozymandias" (1818), two vast, trunkless legs of stone stand in the desert. The pedestal boasts: "Look on my works, ye Mighty, and despair!" Then the traveller adds: "Nothing beside remains." Britannica reads the ruin as a ruler's power vanquished by time. The statue never says so. It doesn't need to.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. To tell them apart, ask one question: does it keep coming back?

cards.headline: A motif keeps coming back
cards.body: A motif is an element (an object, image, sound, idea or word) that recurs through a work and points toward its theme. A symbol can appear just once; a motif must recur. Remember Level 25's Poe story? The old man's heartbeat maddens the narrator before the murder, and he still hears it afterward, until he confesses. Each return tightens the screw.

title: The Hero's Journey
objective: After this level you can trace the stages of Joseph Campbell's hero's journey through a familiar story.
summary: Campbell's monomyth (1949): separation, initiation, return, in 17 stages from the Call to Adventure to Freedom to Live. Gilgamesh wins his boon and loses it.

cards.headline: One scholar claimed the world's heroes all walk the same road.
cards.body: In 1949, Joseph Campbell published The Hero with a Thousand Faces. He argued that the world's myths share one basic story, which he called the monomyth. You may know it by another name: the hero's journey.

cards.headline: Out, through, and back
cards.body: At the core are three movements: separation, initiation and return. The hero sets out from the everyday world, has transformative adventures, and comes home, bringing back a boon. George Lucas drew on the book for Star Wars. Leave, be tested, return changed: once you know it, you'll spot it.

cards.headline: Seventeen stages, three acts
cards.body: Campbell lays out 17 stages. Departure has 5, opening with the Call to Adventure, the Refusal of the Call, Supernatural Aid and the Crossing of the First Threshold. Initiation has 6, from the Road of Trials to the Ultimate Boon. Return has 6, ending with Freedom to Live.

cards.headline: Try it on Gilgamesh
cards.body: Enkidu's death is the call: it sends the king on a dangerous journey to Utnapishtim, to learn how to escape death. He finds a plant that renews youth, a boon if ever there was one. Then a serpent seizes it, and he returns to Uruk still mortal. A caution: critics argue Campbell's links between myths rest on his own interpretation.

title: Genre: Knowing What to Expect
objective: After this level you can explain how a genre sets up promises that readers expect a story to keep or cleverly break.
summary: A genre is a kind of work with conventions readers expect. Austen's Northanger Abbey sets up Gothic promises and breaks them: the secret manuscript is a washing bill.

cards.headline: A young reader goes looking for a Gothic secret and finds laundry.
cards.body: In Jane Austen's Northanger Abbey (published 1817), Catherine Morland has been reading Gothic novels like Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho. At the abbey she finds a mysterious roll of old papers. By daylight she sees she "held a washing-bill in her hand."

cards.headline: A genre is a kind
cards.body: Genre, from a French word for "kind", is a type or category of literary work, like the epic, tragedy, comedy, novel or short story. Genres are recognized by their recurring conventions, purposes and audience expectations. Level 2's fable is one: animals that talk and act like people, a poke at human folly, and a moral, often at the end.

cards.headline: Promises to keep, or to break
cards.body: Those conventions work like promises: audiences expect them kept. Writers can follow the conventions, or manipulate them on purpose. Northanger Abbey does the second. It's a satire that subverts the popular plot devices of Gothic fiction: haunted castles, the supernatural, a central mystery, suspense. The joke works only because you know the promise.

cards.fact: She even suspects a murder.
cards.context: Catherine becomes convinced that General Tilney murdered his wife, until his son Henry firmly sets her straight. Catherine has to learn that she is in a different kind of book.

title: Checkpoint: How Stories Work
objective: After this level you can take any story apart into its plot, conflict, characters, narrator and theme.
summary: Forster: a story is events in time order; a plot adds cause ("of grief"). The toolkit got its names from 1863 to 1961. Try it on Aesop's fox.

cards.headline: The king died, and then...
cards.body: Forster: "The king died and then the queen died" is a story, events in their time sequence. "The king died, and then the queen died of grief" is a plot: the emphasis falls on causality. Two words, "of grief", turn a list into a reason. Every tool in this chapter asks the same question underneath: why?

mascot.line: Five questions open any story: what happens, what's in the way, who changes, who's telling it, and what it means.

title: What Makes a Poem a Poem
objective: After this level you can explain how line breaks, compression and sound set poetry apart from prose.
summary: A poem leans on the line: end-stopped or enjambed, as in Williams's "a red wheel / barrow." Poetry concentrates meaning, is built for sound and predates literacy.

cards.headline: The best words in the best order: a poet's recipe from 1827.
cards.body: Samuel Taylor Coleridge offered two definitions. Prose: "words in their best order." Poetry: "the best words in the best order." Neat, but it leaves the real question open. What does a poem do that a paragraph doesn't? Three things: it breaks into lines, it packs meaning tight, and it's built for the ear.

cards.headline: The line is the first signal
cards.body: Formally, what sets poetry apart is the line: poems lean on it far more than prose does. A line can stop at punctuation (end-stopped) or let its sentence run on across the break. That run-on is enjambment, from the French for "to stride over." In 1923, William Carlos Williams split a single word across a break: "a red wheel / barrow." The break slows you down and fixes the picture in your mind. One line break, one wheelbarrow, twice the attention.
cards.callout: Enjambment: a sentence strides over the line break.

mascot.line: This is Level 1's oral literature again: poems began as voices. When a poem puzzles you, read it out loud.

cards.headline: Packed tight, made for the ear
cards.body: Britannica calls poetry language that gives a concentrated awareness of experience, chosen and arranged for its meaning, sound and rhythm. Concentrated is the word to keep: a poem squeezes a lot into a little. Sound matters because poetry is older than reading. It predates literacy and comes before prose in every literature. So when a poem puzzles you, don't just stare at it. Say it.

title: Rhythm and Meter
objective: After this level you can hear stressed and unstressed syllables and recognize iambic pentameter.
summary: Meter counts stresses in feet: an iamb rises (to-DAY), a trochee falls (MAT-ter). Five iambs make iambic pentameter, Shakespeare's line; unrhymed, it is blank verse.

cards.headline: Say "today" out loud. You just spoke an iamb.
cards.body: You didn't say TO-day. You said to-DAY: a soft beat, then a strong one. English is full of these ups and downs, and poets have been counting them for centuries. The counting has a name.

cards.headline: A ruler for the ear
cards.body: Meter, from the Greek metron, "measure," is the measured pattern of stresses in a line of verse. Poets count it in feet: small units of stressed and unstressed syllables. An iamb goes da-DUM, like "today." A trochee flips it, DUM-da, like "matter." Greek prefixes then count the feet in a line: tetrameter has four, pentameter five, hexameter six.

cards.headline: Five iambs in a row
cards.body: Line up five iambs and you get iambic pentameter: about ten syllables that rise five times. Shakespeare wrote his sonnets in it, and most of the verse in his plays. Hear it in Sonnet 73: "that TIME of YEAR thou MAYST in ME be-HOLD." Drop the rhyme and it becomes blank verse, the standard line for Shakespeare and for John Milton. Five soft-loud steps, and you're speaking in Shakespeare's rhythm.

cards.fact: Flip the foot and the beat lands first.
cards.context: Not every poem rises. Edgar Allan Poe's "The Raven" runs on trochees, stress first: DUM-da, DUM-da. William Blake wrote in trochaic meter too. Hold on to Blake: he comes back at the end of this chapter, and you'll hear the difference the moment you read him aloud.

title: Rhyme, Alliteration and Sound
objective: After this level you can identify rhyme, slant rhyme, alliteration and assonance and how each ties words together.
summary: Rhyme matches sounds at line ends, perfectly (bright, flight) or on a slant (young, long). Alliteration repeats first consonants; assonance repeats vowel sounds.

cards.headline: Shakespeare's Sonnet 30 is full of s sounds, on purpose.
cards.body: "When to the sessions of sweet silent thought / I summon up remembrance of things past." Sessions, sweet, silent, summon. Say it aloud and the words start echoing each other. Poets have a whole kit for making words chime, and you can learn to hear every tool in it.

cards.headline: Rhyme, perfect and slant
cards.body: Rhyme is the matching of sounds, usually at the ends of lines. In a perfect rhyme, the last stressed vowel and everything after it match: bright and flight. A slant rhyme only nearly matches, like young and long. Rhyme is younger than you might think. Ancient Greek and Roman poets rarely if ever used it, and it took hold in Western poetry only in the Middle Ages. China's earliest surviving rhymes date to about the 10th century BCE.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. Alliteration: consonants, usually at the front. Assonance: vowels, anywhere nearby.

cards.headline: Echoes at the front and in the middle
cards.body: Alliteration repeats consonant sounds, especially at the start of nearby words: sessions of sweet silent thought. Its sounds are pleasing and memorable, which is why nursery rhymes and ads love it. Assonance repeats vowel sounds in nearby words; its Latin root, assonare, means "to answer with the same sound." So rhyme ties line endings together, alliteration ties word beginnings, and assonance ties the vowels in between.

objective: After this level you can tell a metaphor from a simile and explain how an image makes a reader feel an idea.
summary: A simile compares with "like" or "as" (Burns's red, red rose); a metaphor speaks as if one thing is another ("All the world's a stage"). Both build imagery for the senses.

cards.headline: Robert Burns compared his love to a rose. One small word does the work.
cards.body: His song opens: "O my Luve's like a red, red rose, / That's newly sprung in June." Notice the "like." Take it out and you get a different kind of comparison. That tiny word is the whole difference between two of poetry's oldest tools.

cards.headline: All the world's a stage
cards.body: Metaphor comes from the Greek metaphora, "a transfer": it carries one thing's qualities over to another. In As You Like It, Shakespeare's Jaques says, "All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players; / They have their exits and their entrances." Not a "like" in sight. For a moment the world simply is a theater, and your life has entrances and exits.

cards.headline: Imagery: ideas you can feel
cards.body: Imagery is language that calls up the senses: sight, sound, smell, touch and taste. Similes and metaphors are two ways to build it. Burns doesn't tell you his love is lovely. He hands you a red, red rose, newly sprung in June, and lets you see it. An image gives you an experience to imagine, not just a statement to accept.

title: The Sonnet
objective: After this level you can explain how a sonnet's 14 lines are built in its Italian and English forms and where its turn comes.
summary: A sonnet is 14 lines of iambic pentameter. The Italian form turns between octave and sestet; the English form, three quatrains and a couplet, turns before the couplet, as in Sonnet 130.

cards.headline: For twelve lines, this love poem refuses to flatter.
cards.body: "My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun; / Coral is far more red, than her lips red." Shakespeare's Sonnet 130 compares his beloved, unfavorably, to all the usual beauties of nature. Then the last two lines swerve. That swerve is the secret engine of the sonnet.

cards.headline: Fourteen lines, a little song
cards.body: A sonnet is a 14-line poem, traditionally in iambic pentameter with a set rhyme scheme. The name comes from the Italian sonetto, "a little sound or song." It began among Sicilian court poets in the 13th century, and the Italian poet Petrarch perfected it. In the 16th century, Sir Thomas Wyatt and Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, brought it to England.

title: Haiku
objective: After this level you can explain how a haiku captures a single moment, using Basho's poem of the old pond and the frog.
summary: A haiku is 17 syllables in 5, 7, 5, grown from the hokku. Basho's 1686 frog poem splits stillness from splash with the cutting word ya, and its frog marks spring.

cards.headline: Basho found the ending of his frog poem first.
cards.body: On a spring day in 1686, frogs kept jumping into the pond in Basho's garden. According to his disciple Shiko, Basho came up with the poem's last two lines first: a frog, the water. Then he needed an opening. What would you pick?

cards.headline: Seventeen syllables, one moment
cards.body: A traditional haiku has 17 syllables in three lines of 5, 7 and 5. It grew from the hokku, the opening stanza of a renga, a long linked poem that several poets wrote by taking turns. In the 17th century, Matsuo Basho raised the hokku into a refined art of its own. Its aim is one brief moment, short enough to read in a single breath.

cards.headline: The old pond
cards.body: Here is what he chose: "furuike ya / kawazu tobikomu / mizu no oto." The old pond, a frog jumps in, the sound of water. Count it: 5, 7, 5. The little word ya is a cutting word, a spoken pause that separates the two halves and joins them: stillness, then splash. And the frog is a season word for spring, so the poem quietly tells you when it happens.

cards.fact: Basho's frog doesn't sing.
cards.context: Classical Japanese poems gave the frog a plaintive singing voice. Basho gave you the sound of a frog jumping into the water instead. No song, no heartbreak: just one plop, in one moment, in an old pond. The whole poem hangs on a sound you've probably heard yourself.

title: Free Verse
objective: After this level you can explain how free verse builds rhythm without regular meter or rhyme.
summary: Free verse drops regular meter for the cadences of speech but keeps the line. Its rhythm comes from patterned sounds, words and phrases, like Whitman's repetitions.

cards.headline: Compose to the musical phrase, not the metronome.
cards.body: That was Ezra Pound's advice to poets: "to compose in the sequence of the musical phrase, not in sequence of a metronome." Level 32's meter ticks along beat after even beat. Pound wanted poems that moved like music instead. Fine slogan. But without a fixed beat, where does the rhythm come from?

cards.headline: Free, not formless
cards.body: Free verse is poetry without a regular meter or set form, shaped instead by the cadences of speech. The name translates the French vers libre, a movement that began in France in the 1880s. Free doesn't mean shapeless, though. Free verse keeps the line, and uses it to set itself apart from prose. Level 31's line breaks still do their work.

cards.headline: Rhythm from repetition
cards.body: Instead of counting syllables, free verse patterns bigger things: sounds, words, phrases, whole sentences. Walt Whitman, the founding father of American free verse, opens Song of Myself: "I celebrate myself, and sing myself, / And what I assume you shall assume." Hear the echoes? Myself, myself. Assume, assume. The repetition is doing the metronome's job.

cards.fact: Free verse has very old roots.
cards.context: One of its greatest ancestors is the poetry of the Psalms and the Song of Songs in the King James Bible. Their parallel lines and sweeping repetitions follow Hebrew cadences, and they inspired poets from William Blake to Whitman. So the "new" freedom of free verse was, in part, a very old sound.

title: The Epic's Toolkit
objective: After this level you can spot the conventions of epic poetry: calling on the Muse, starting in the middle and the long epic simile.
summary: Epics call on the Muse ("Sing, O goddess"), begin in medias res (the Iliad opens in the war's last year) and stretch comparisons into epic similes.

cards.headline: Homer doesn't start the Trojan War from the egg.
cards.body: The Roman poet Horace praised Homer for skipping the story's very beginning, ab ovo, "from the egg" (the egg from which Helen was born). Instead, Homer hurries his listener straight into the middle of things. Epics run on a few habits like that. Here are three.

cards.headline: Sing, Muse
cards.body: Epics often open with an invocation: the poet calls on a Muse or god for inspiration. In Samuel Butler's translations, the Iliad begins, "Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus," and the Odyssey, "Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero." Centuries later, John Milton kept the habit in Paradise Lost: "Sing, Heavenly Muse." One line in, and you know you're in an epic.

cards.headline: Into the middle of things
cards.body: Epics also begin in medias res, Latin for "into the middle of things": they plunge into a crucial moment in a chain of events. The Iliad doesn't retell the whole Trojan War. It covers a few crucial weeks in the war's final year and focuses on one thing: the wrath of Achilles. You arrive mid-war, with no egg in sight.

mascot.line: It connects: an epic simile is Level 34's simile, just given room to breathe.

cards.headline: The simile that keeps going
cards.body: The third tool is the epic simile: a comparison stretched over several lines, used to raise the heroic scene. In Butler's Iliad: "As when the rising west wind furs the face of the sea and the waters grow dark beneath it, so sat the companies of Trojans and Achaeans upon the plain." Two armies sitting down become the sea darkening under the wind.

title: Aristotle's Rules of Tragedy
objective: After this level you can explain Aristotle's ideas of the tragic hero's error, the reversal, the recognition and catharsis.
summary: Aristotle's tragic hero falls by an error (hamartia). Reversal flips the action and recognition turns ignorance to knowledge, together in Oedipus; pity and fear bring catharsis.

cards.headline: A messenger brings good news. It turns into the worst news.
cards.body: In the Greek tragedy of Oedipus, a messenger comes to cheer Oedipus and free him from his fears about his mother. But by revealing who Oedipus really is, he produces the opposite effect. The philosopher Aristotle, in his Poetics, used this scene to explain how tragedy works.

cards.headline: An error, not a villain
cards.body: Aristotle wanted a hero who is not simply good, someone "highly renowned and prosperous" who falls "not by vice or depravity, but by some error or frailty" (in S. H. Butcher's translation). His word was hamartia, from a Greek verb meaning "to err." He meant an error of judgment; later critics turned it into a moral flaw, like jealousy. Oedipus unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother.

cards.headline: Reversal and recognition
cards.body: Aristotle named two turning points. Peripeteia, the reversal, is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite: the cheering messenger. Anagnorisis, the recognition, is a change from ignorance to knowledge. The best recognition, he said, comes together with the reversal, as in Oedipus. The moment he learns who he is, his fortune flips.
cards.callout: Reversal: the action flips. Recognition: ignorance becomes knowledge.

cards.headline: Why watch? Catharsis
cards.body: Aristotle defined tragedy as an imitation of a serious action that, "through pity and fear," effects "the proper purgation of these emotions." The Greek word is catharsis: purgation or purification. Does tragedy flush feelings out, like medicine, or cleanse us, more like a ritual? Scholars still argue. No single reading has won.

title: Checkpoint: How Poetry and Drama Work
objective: After this level you can read a short poem or scene for its meter, sound, imagery and dramatic shape.
summary: Blake's The Tyger (1794) puts the toolkit to work: a mostly trochaic beat, rhyme and alliteration, forge imagery, and a one-word turn from "Could" to "Dare".

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: one poem, every tool.
cards.body: You now carry a reader's toolkit: lines, meter, sound, images and turns. Let's open one famous poem, William Blake's The Tyger, and use them all.

cards.headline: Listen first
cards.body: Blake published The Tyger in 1794, in Songs of Innocence and of Experience. It opens: "Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night." Read it aloud. Critics hear its lines as mostly trochaic: four beats that start on the stress, TY-ger TY-ger BURN-ing BRIGHT. Bright rhymes with night, and the next question alliterates: "Could frame thy fearful symmetry?"

cards.headline: Then see the images
cards.body: The poem asks who could have made such a beast, and it pictures the making as metalwork: "What the hammer? what the chain, / In what furnace was thy brain?" The tiger is forged like molten metal at an anvil. That's imagery you can feel: the heat of a furnace, the ring of a hammer.

cards.headline: Find the turn
cards.body: Last, the shape. The poem is a series of questions that never get answered, including "Did he who made the Lamb make thee?" The final stanza repeats the first, with one word changed: "Could frame" becomes "Dare frame." Like a sonnet's volta, a single word turns the thought, from what was possible to what took daring.

title: Antigone: Law Against Conscience
objective: After this level you can explain why Sophocles' Antigone, a clash between a ruler's law and a sister's duty to the dead, is still staged.
summary: In Sophocles' Antigone, Creon forbids burying Polyneices and Antigone buries him anyway. Law against conscience still speaks, as Anouilh's 1944 Paris version showed.

cards.headline: The law says leave the body. His sister buries it anyway.
cards.body: In Sophocles' Antigone, Creon, king of Thebes, forbids the burial of Polyneices, who attacked the city. Antigone, his sister, buries him anyway. The play is ancient. So why do theaters keep putting it on?

cards.headline: Two duties, one body
cards.body: Antigone was probably first performed around 442 BCE, and its conflict is easy to state and hard to settle. On one side stands law: Creon's edict that enemies of the state must not be buried. On the other stands conscience: Antigone's duty to give her brother a proper burial. Each side has a valid claim. That's what makes it a tragedy and not a lecture.

cards.headline: The gods take a side
cards.body: Creon holds to state law so rigidly that he defies the gods, denying the duty every person owes the dead. The prophet Tiresias finally persuades him to relent, but too late. Antigone has already killed herself, and Creon's son Haemon and then his wife Eurydice take their own lives. The king who put his law above everything is left alone with it.

cards.fact: In 1944, Antigone's refusal returned to the stage in occupied Paris.
cards.context: Jean Anouilh's French version of the play opened in Paris on 6 February 1944, during the Nazi occupation. A ruler's decree against one person's conscience: the ancient clash fit a city under occupation. That's why Antigone keeps coming back. Wherever a law and a conscience collide, the play is already written.

title: Li Bai, Du Fu and Tang Poetry
objective: After this level you can explain why the Tang dynasty is called the golden age of Chinese poetry.
summary: Under the Tang (618 to 907), officials were hired through literary exams and nearly 49,000 poems survive. Li Bai wrote freely of wine and the Moon; Du Fu mastered regulated verse.

cards.headline: The poet many call China's greatest failed his exam.
cards.body: Du Fu received a traditional Confucian education, then failed the imperial examinations of 735. He lived under the Tang dynasty, when poetry was the period's greatest glory. How did one dynasty turn out so much poetry?

cards.headline: A dynasty that ran on verse
cards.body: The Tang dynasty ran from 618 to 907, and it's often called the golden age of Chinese literature. More than 48,900 poems by more than 2,200 Tang poets survive. One reason: the Tang expanded exams in literature and culture for hiring officials, so a way with words could open a career. When the state recruits by the pen, pens get busy.

cards.headline: Li Bai breaks the rules
cards.body: A popular Tang form was lüshi, regulated verse: eight lines of five or seven syllables, set to strict tonal patterns. Li Bai (701 to 762) avoided it. A romantic, he chose freer forms to celebrate wine, friendship, solitude and nature. Popular tradition says he drowned when, drunk in a boat, he tried to seize the Moon's reflection. A legend, but a fitting one.

cards.headline: Du Fu masters them
cards.body: Du Fu (712 to 770) went the other way: he refined regulated verse to a point of glowing intensity. Then in 755 An Lushan's rebellion broke out, and Du Fu lived through poverty and exile. His poems turned to people caught in war, with deep compassion. Many critics call him China's greatest poet. Li Bai looks up at the Moon; Du Fu looks at the people on the road.

title: Journey to the West
objective: After this level you can explain why the Monkey King's pilgrimage to India became one of China's best-loved novels.
summary: Journey to the West, a 100-chapter Ming novel, sends the real monk Xuanzang to India with Monkey, Pigsy and Sandy. Its comedy, satire and rebel Monkey King made it beloved.

cards.headline: A monk walked to India for books. The novel gave him a monkey.
cards.body: The Buddhist monk Xuanzang really made a pilgrimage to India in the 7th century, in search of sacred texts. One of China's best-loved novels sends him again, with a bodyguard born from a stone egg. Why did this version win so many hearts?

cards.headline: A real road, an invented crew
cards.body: Journey to the West is a 100-chapter novel from China's Ming dynasty, usually credited to Wu Cheng'en. It keeps the real journey of Xuanzang (602 to 664), called Tripitaka here, and gives him three animal spirits as companions: the magically gifted Monkey, the clumsy Pigsy and the fish spirit Sandy. Together they get through 81 adventures on the road. A pilgrimage, turned into a road trip with demons.

cards.headline: The Monkey who fought heaven
cards.body: The novel begins with Monkey, Sun Wukong, born from a stone egg. He gains magic powers: he shape-shifts and somersaults through clouds. He challenges the Jade Emperor's authority until the Buddha subdues him and imprisons him beneath the Five Elements Mountain. Freed through the bodhisattva Guanyin, he agrees to protect the monk, and by the end he attains Buddhahood. Rebel first, then pilgrim.

cards.headline: Why readers love it
cards.body: Part of the appeal is pure fun: fights, tricks and transformations. But the novel also carries biting satire of society and Chinese bureaucracy, and it can be read as an allegory. English readers got Arthur Waley's abridged translation, titled simply Monkey, in 1942. Comedy on top, a sharp point underneath: that's a recipe that lasts.

title: The Tale of Genji
objective: After this level you can explain why Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji is often called the world's first novel.
summary: Murasaki Shikibu, a court lady, finished The Tale of Genji about 1010. Hiragana let Heian women write, and its 54 chapters of inner life are why it's often called the first novel.

cards.headline: About 1010, a court lady finished what's often called the first novel.
cards.body: She was Murasaki Shikibu, and she wrote The Tale of Genji while serving at the Japanese court. Why does a book that old get that title? Start with who got to write what.

cards.headline: The script that let women write
cards.body: We don't know her real name. We do know she learned Chinese, then generally the exclusive sphere of men. At the Heian court, men composed official documents in stilted Chinese. Hiragana, a script for writing Japanese, gave court women their chance to create works of literature. The men kept the official language. The women got the stories.

mascot.line: Keep the hedge: Genji is often called the first novel. Scholars argue about firsts, so say it that way too.

cards.headline: One life, 54 chapters
cards.body: Genji follows one character and his legacy through 54 chapters. The hero is a handsome, sensitive, gifted courtier, an excellent lover and a worthy friend. The book shows supreme sensitivity to human emotions and to nature, and as it goes on, its tone darkens, reflecting the Buddhist conviction that this world doesn't last. A long story that follows inner lives over time: that's what a novel does.

cards.headline: From heroes to people

He's a lover and a friend at court, and the book is an absorbing picture of Heian aristocrats: their entertainment, dress, daily life and moral code. A hero's story with the heroics left out.

title: The Thousand and One Nights
objective: After this level you can explain why Scheherazade tells her stories and how a frame story holds many tales together.
summary: Scheherazade saves her life by leaving each night's story unfinished: a frame story holding many tales. The Nights kept growing; Aladdin came from Aleppo's Hanna Diyab in 1709.

cards.headline: Her life depended on a cliffhanger.
cards.body: In the frame story of The Thousand and One Nights, King Shahryar, after discovering his wife's infidelity, marries a new wife each day and has her killed. Then Scheherazade marries him, armed with nothing but stories.

cards.headline: Stop at the best part
cards.body: Each evening Scheherazade tells the king a story and leaves it unfinished, promising the ending the next night. He wants to know what happens, so he puts off her execution day after day. In the end, he abandons his cruel plan altogether. It's the oldest reason to keep listening: you have to find out what happens next.

cards.headline: A story that holds stories
cards.body: Scheherazade's situation is a frame story: an overall, unifying story within which other tales are told. The frame gives every tale a reason to be told, and it can hold as many as the teller can supply, one night at a time. Think of the frame as a bookshelf. Keep adding books, and the shelf still holds them together.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: Aladdin wasn't in the old Arabic Nights. He reached the book in Paris, told by a storyteller from Aleppo.

cards.headline: A collection that kept growing
cards.body: The Nights draws on stories from India, Iran, Iraq, Egypt, Turkey and possibly Greece, and its Persian source was called A Thousand Tales. Europe met it in Antoine Galland's French translation, published from 1704 to 1717. The tales best known in the West, like Aladdin and Ali Baba, were later additions. In Paris in 1709, Hanna Diyab, a young Syrian from Aleppo, told Galland stories, Aladdin among them, that fed his last volumes.

title: The Shahnameh
objective: After this level you can explain why Ferdowsi's Book of Kings is credited with keeping the Persian language alive.
summary: Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (finished 1010) runs from Iran's myths to the Arab conquest. Written in nearly pure Persian when Arabic dominated writing, it's credited with keeping Persian alive.

cards.headline: One poem is credited with keeping a language alive.
cards.body: Ferdowsi completed the Shahnameh, the Book of Kings, in 1010. It's the Persian national epic. How could a single poem help save a whole language?

cards.headline: A nation's memory in verse
cards.body: Ferdowsi gave the Persian national epic its final and enduring form. The Shahnameh runs from Iran's mythical times down to the Arab conquest of the 7th century, and it's a mixture of myth, legend and history. One poem holds a whole nation's past, the way a family album holds generations.

cards.headline: A father, a son, a fight
cards.body: The poem's first section is entirely legendary, and its most famous story is a tragedy. The great hero Rostam fights his own son, Sohrab, and the fight ends with the father unwittingly killing his son. All of the hero's strength, turned against his own family: that's the epic's great heartbreak.

cards.headline: Why it's credited with saving Persian
cards.body: Arabic once held a monopoly on writing in the Muslim world. Persian was the first language to break through it, emerging again as a written language in the 9th century. Ferdowsi's epic, based on a Middle Persian original, is pure Persian with only the slightest admixture of Arabic, and it quickly became Iranians' literary expression of their national feeling. The stories and the language survived together, in one book.
