title: Beowulf
objective: After this level you can explain why Beowulf, which survives in a single manuscript, matters as the great epic of Old English.
summary: Beowulf fights Grendel, Grendel's mother and a dragon. The poem, Old English literature's highest achievement, survives in one manuscript of about 1000 that came through a 1731 fire.

cards.headline: The only copy of Old English's great epic has been through a fire.
cards.body: Beowulf survives in a single manuscript, made around the year 1000. In 1731 fire damaged it, but much of its text is still readable. Had it burned, the poem would simply be gone.

cards.headline: A hero, two monsters and a dragon
cards.body: The poem is set in early 6th-century Scandinavia, mostly in what are now Denmark and Sweden. At King Hrothgar's hall, Heorot, Beowulf fights the monster Grendel, then Grendel's mother. Much later, after ruling in peace for 50 years, the old king faces a fire-breathing dragon, and the fight costs him his life. Young hero, old hero: the poem gives you both.

mascot.line: This is Level 10's lesson again: stories survive by memory, copying and luck. Beowulf's one copy used up a lot of luck.

cards.fact: Every edition of Beowulf goes back to one manuscript.
cards.context: Nobody knows exactly when the poem was composed; some scholars think the 8th century. The one copy, catalogued today as Cotton MS Vitellius A XV, was made around the year 1000. It was damaged by fire in 1731, yet much of its text remains readable. No backup, no second copy.

cards.headline: Why it matters
cards.body: Beowulf is the highest achievement of Old English literature and the earliest European vernacular epic: a long heroic poem in a people's own language rather than Latin. Lose that one manuscript, and Old English would lose its highest achievement.

title: Dante's Divine Comedy
objective: After this level you can explain why Dante wrote his journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise in Italian rather than Latin.
summary: Dante's Divine Comedy (about 1308 to 1321) leads through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise with Virgil and Beatrice. Writing in Italian, not Latin, reached a wider audience and changed Italian.

cards.headline: Midway through life, a poet finds himself lost in a dark forest.
cards.body: That's how Dante's Divine Comedy begins. In Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's translation: "Midway upon the journey of our life / I found myself within a forest dark, / For the straightforward pathway had been lost." From there, the road leads through the whole afterlife. And Dante told it in Italian, not Latin. Why?

cards.headline: Hell, Purgatory, Paradise
cards.body: Written in Italian from about 1308 to 1321, the poem has 100 cantos in three sections: Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso. The Roman poet Virgil guides Dante down through Hell and up to the summit of Purgatory, where Beatrice takes over and leads him through Paradise. Its rhyme scheme, terza rima, runs in three-line stanzas. A tour of the whole afterlife, with a famous poet as your guide.

cards.headline: Why not Latin?
cards.body: Dante chose to write in the Italian vernacular, the language people spoke, rather than in Latin. That choice ensured his poem would reach a wider audience, and it lent a voice to the emerging lay culture of his country, people outside the clergy. You didn't need a Latin education to follow Dante into Hell.

cards.fact: Dante's choice changed the Italian language itself.
cards.context: Writing in Italian rather than Latin had a revolutionary impact on the development of the Italian language and on Western literature. It decisively influenced the course of literary development. The everyday language had climbed all the way to Paradise.

title: The Canterbury Tales
objective: After this level you can explain why Chaucer's pilgrims telling stories in English made a landmark of English literature.
summary: Chaucer's pilgrims tell tales on the road to Canterbury for a free supper: a frame for every kind of story. He wrote in English while Gower also wrote in French and Latin.

cards.headline: A storytelling contest, and the prize is a free supper.
cards.body: About 30 pilgrims gather at the Tabard Inn in Southwark, bound for Becket's shrine at Canterbury. The Host proposes a contest: tell tales on the road, and the best one wins a free supper. That's the setup of Geoffrey Chaucer's Canterbury Tales.

cards.headline: Another frame, a new cast
cards.body: Chaucer wrote the Tales between 1387 and 1400. Like the Nights in Level 45, they sit inside a frame story. But this frame is a pilgrimage, and it brings together varied tellers who emerge as vivid personalities. Chaucer died with the work unfinished: 24 tales, some of them incomplete. The road to Canterbury never quite ends.

cards.headline: Everyone gets a turn
cards.body: The pilgrims range from a knight to a miller, the Wife of Bath and a pardoner. Their tales range too: courtly romance, fabliau, a saint's life, even a beast fable. Because the pilgrims, not Chaucer, tell the tales, he gained an unprecedented freedom to try many genres. The poet John Dryden later summed it up: "here is God's plenty."

cards.headline: Why English?
cards.body: Chaucer's contemporary John Gower wrote two of his weighty works in French and Latin. Chaucer was doubtless as fluent in French as in the English of his day, and his early poems leaned on fashionable French love poetry. Scholars admit his decision to write in English isn't easy to explain. But he made it, and the outstanding English poet before Shakespeare has been called "the first finder of our language."

title: Shakespeare's Globe
objective: After this level you can explain why Shakespeare wrote plays that could hold a whole crowd, from standing groundlings to nobles.
summary: The Globe (1599) was open to the sky: a penny to stand among the groundlings, more for the galleries. Every class came, so Shakespeare put clowns in tragedies and kings in comedies.

cards.headline: In Hamlet, Shakespeare pokes fun at his cheapest customers.
cards.body: Hamlet scolds actors who overdo a scene "to split the ears of the groundlings". The groundlings were real people: the playgoers who paid least and stood in the yard around the stage. So who else was in Shakespeare's crowd, and how did one play hold them all?

cards.headline: A penny to stand
cards.body: Shakespeare's company opened the Globe on London's Bankside in 1599, built from the timbers of their old playhouse, the Theatre. The yard around the stage had only the sky for a roof. A penny bought you a standing place there, among the groundlings. Another penny bought a bench in the galleries, and the Lords' Rooms cost most. At a hit, two or three thousand people squeezed in.

cards.headline: Porters, apprentices and royalty
cards.body: Playgoers came from nearly every class. A visitor in 1617 described the crowd around the stage as porters and carters. Servants and apprentices spent their spare time there, wealthier people filled the seats, and royalty loved a play too. Shakespeare wrote for them all.
cards.callout: Every class, one play: that was the job.

cards.headline: Clowns in the tragedies
cards.body: So he mixed. Shakespeare put clowns in his tragedies and kings in his comedies. Some of his most popular clowns turn up in his darkest plays: the gravediggers in Hamlet, the Porter in Macbeth. And because the stage had little or no scenery, the words did the work, telling the crowd where each scene took place. Something for the yard and something for the galleries, in the same play.

title: Hamlet and the Soliloquy
objective: After this level you can explain why the soliloquy lets an audience hear a character think, using Hamlet.
summary: Hamlet hides his thoughts from the court behind a show of madness. Only his soliloquies, speeches spoken alone on stage, let the audience hear what he really thinks and plans.

cards.headline: Hamlet hides what he thinks from everyone. Except you.
cards.body: Early in the play, Hamlet tells the court he has "that within which passeth show": an inner self no outward show can express. Then he starts acting mad on purpose. The people around him can't read his mind. The audience can, thanks to one old stage device.

cards.headline: A ghost, a murder, a mask
cards.body: In Hamlet, written about 1599 to 1601, the ghost of Hamlet's father says he was poisoned by his brother Claudius. Claudius has since married Hamlet's mother, Gertrude, and taken the crown. Hamlet's answer is to put "an antic disposition" on: a show of madness to deceive Claudius and the court. From here on, everyone on stage is watching a mask.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. Aside: a quick line the others don't hear. Soliloquy: alone on stage, thinking at length.

cards.headline: Thinking out loud
cards.body: A soliloquy is a speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud while alone on stage, or while the others keep silent. The word joins Latin solus, "alone", and loqui, "to speak". Don't confuse it with an aside: a brief remark the audience hears but the other characters supposedly don't. An aside is a quick glance at the audience; a soliloquy is a whole mind at work.

cards.headline: What only you hear
cards.body: Alone at the end of Act 2, Hamlet drops the mask. He fears the ghost may be the devil, so he plans a test: actors will stage a murder like his father's in front of Claudius. "The play's the thing / Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the King." In Act 3 comes "To be, or not to be", Shakespeare's most famous soliloquy, as Hamlet weighs whether it's nobler to suffer life's troubles or fight them. Claudius never hears a word. You hear all of it.

title: Romeo and Juliet's Borrowed Plot
objective: After this level you can explain why Shakespeare borrowed his plots and what he added to them, using Romeo and Juliet.
summary: Romeo and Juliet came from Arthur Brooke's 1562 poem, with Ovid's Pyramus and Thisbe behind it. Borrowing was normal; Shakespeare's changes (four days, Mercutio, sympathy) made it his.

cards.headline: Shakespeare gives away the ending before the play begins.
cards.body: Romeo and Juliet opens with a Prologue announcing that "A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life". No twist, no surprise: you know how it ends before anyone has fallen in love. So why would a crowd stay to watch?

cards.headline: A borrowed story
cards.body: Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet about 1594 to 1596. His main source was Arthur Brooke's long poem The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet (1562), itself based on a French version of an Italian tale by Matteo Bandello. Further back stands Ovid's Pyramus and Thisbe from Level 7, one inspiration for the play, which Shakespeare also turned into a farce in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

cards.headline: Nobody wanted a new plot
cards.body: That wasn't cheating. Playwrights of the time weren't too bothered about being original: they reworked old stories and even used other people's plots. With a few exceptions, Shakespeare didn't invent the plots of his plays. The question wasn't what happens. It was how well you could tell it.
cards.callout: Borrowing plots was normal; the telling was the craft.

cards.headline: What he added
cards.body: Put the versions side by side. Brooke's story takes at least nine months; Shakespeare crams it into four days, Sunday to Thursday morning. In Brooke, Mercutio is just a guest at Capulet's feast; Shakespeare gives him the Queen Mab speech, the jokes and his death. And Brooke's preface condemns the lovers as a warning to youth who neglect their parents' authority. Shakespeare doesn't follow his lead.

title: Disguises and Weddings: Comedies
objective: After this level you can explain why Shakespeare's comedies run on disguise and mistaken identity and end in marriage.
summary: In Twelfth Night and As You Like It, heroines disguised as young men tie the plot in knots. The audience knows the secret (dramatic irony) until the truth comes out and the weddings begin.

cards.headline: In Twelfth Night, one actor was a boy playing a girl playing a boy.
cards.body: In Shakespeare's England, women's roles were played by boys. So Viola, a young woman who disguises herself as a young man, was a boy playing a girl playing a boy for most of the play. Shakespeare's comedies love this kind of tangle. What does it do for them?

cards.headline: A disguise ties the knot
cards.body: In Twelfth Night (about 1600 to 1602), twins Viola and Sebastian are parted by a shipwreck, each thinking the other drowned. Viola disguises herself as a young man, Cesario, and serves Duke Orsino. Orsino sends Cesario to woo Countess Olivia for him, and Olivia falls in love with the messenger. Viola, stuck in the middle, sighs: "O time, thou must untangle this, not I".

cards.headline: You know; they don't
cards.body: Here's the fuel. Dramatic irony is when the audience understands more than the characters do, so their words carry a double meaning. You know Cesario is Viola; Olivia doesn't. In As You Like It (about 1598 to 1600), Rosalind, disguised as a young man called Ganymede, even gets lovesick Orlando to woo her as if she were Rosalind. He thinks it's practice. You know it's the real thing.
cards.callout: Disguise gives the audience a secret the characters don't share.

cards.headline: Then the weddings
cards.body: In Twelfth Night, Sebastian's return piles mistaken identity on mistaken identity, until the twins stand together, the truth comes out and the lovers pair off. Shakespeare's comedies, for all their bickering and mix-ups, frequently end with the promise of a wedding, sometimes several. The disguise ties the knot; the reveal unties it.

title: Words Shakespeare Gave Us
objective: After this level you can explain why so many everyday words and phrases are first recorded in Shakespeare, and what "first recorded" means.
summary: Many words and phrases, like the green-eyed monster, are first recorded in Shakespeare. That means the earliest written use found so far, not proof he coined them: earlier uses keep turning up.

cards.headline: Feeling jealous? You may be quoting Iago.
cards.body: In Othello, Iago warns: "beware, my lord, of jealousy; / It is the green-ey'd monster". People still call jealousy the green-eyed monster. Like "sour grapes" from Aesop's fable in Level 2, a phrase has escaped its story and moved into everyday speech.

cards.headline: A mountain of firsts
cards.body: Shakespeare's works give the first recorded use of a great many English words. He may have made plenty of them himself, by combining words, turning nouns into verbs, or adding prefixes and suffixes. He was the first writer on record, for instance, to use partner, property and scissor as verbs. The words already existed; he put them to new work.

mascot.line: Keep this: first recorded means the oldest example found so far. A new search can always push the date back.

cards.headline: First recorded isn't first said
cards.body: Careful, though. A word's earliest known use means the earliest evidence found so far, not the day it was invented. The Oxford English Dictionary's original editors and hundreds of volunteer readers recorded Shakespeare's language in more detail than any other writer's, so his uses were the ones they found. Look where they looked less, and older uses turn up: assassination, in Macbeth, appears in a 1572 letter by the diplomat Sir Thomas Smith.

cards.headline: Words that wander
cards.body: Some phrases survive while their meaning moves. In Romeo and Juliet, Mercutio jokes about a "wild-goose chase": a horse race in which the leader chose any course and the others had to follow. Today a wild-goose chase means a fruitless search. The words stayed; the race was forgotten.

title: Don Quixote
objective: After this level you can explain why Cervantes' tale of a man who reads too many knightly romances is called the first modern novel.
summary: Cervantes' Don Quixote (1605, 1615) parodies knightly romances: a reader-turned-knight charges windmills beside proverb-loving Sancho. Its clashing voices make it a prototype of the modern novel.

cards.headline: A man reads so many knight stories that he becomes a knight. Or tries to.
cards.body: An aging Spanish gentleman is so enamoured of chivalric romances, tales of knights errant, that he loses his wits. He takes the name Don Quixote, recruits a peasant named Sancho Panza as his squire, and rides out as a wandering knight.

cards.headline: Giants, or windmills?
cards.body: Miguel de Cervantes published Don Quixote in two parts, in 1605 and 1615. It began as a parody of the chivalric romances then in fashion. In its most famous scene, Don Quixote sees a row of windmills, decides they are giants, and charges. The romances promised giants. Spain offered windmills.

cards.headline: Two voices on one road
cards.body: What keeps the book moving is talk. Sancho Panza, a short, earthy peasant famous for his proverbs, meets his master's lofty idealism with common sense, and Cervantes built much of the story on their relationship. Around them, the book fills with characters of different beliefs and points of view: the multiple voices modern fiction depends on.
cards.callout: Idealism and common sense, arguing on horseback.

cards.headline: A novel that knows it's a novel
cards.body: In Part 2, Don Quixote meets people who have already read Part 1 and know all about him, and some use it to play tricks on him. A spurious sequel by one Avellaneda had appeared in 1614, and Cervantes answered it inside his own story. Its many voices make Don Quixote a prototype of the modern novel. It is often called the first.

title: Why the Novel Took Off
objective: After this level you can explain why the novel boomed in 18th-century Britain, from Robinson Crusoe onward.
summary: Robinson Crusoe (1719) posed as a castaway's own true story in plain, concrete detail. A wider middle-class readership, many of them women, and lending libraries made novels boom.

cards.headline: The word novel comes from a word for "new".
cards.body: It's a shortened form of the Italian novella, from Latin novus, "new". In 18th-century Britain, a new kind of book took off, led by a castaway whose story claimed to be "Written by Himself". Why then, and why there?

cards.headline: A castaway's memoir, invented
cards.body: Daniel Defoe was 59 when he published his first novel, Robinson Crusoe, in 1719. Its title page presented the story as "Written by Himself", as if Crusoe were a real sailor telling the truth. Defoe's style is plain and matter-of-fact, full of vivid, concrete detail: Crusoe builds a raft to strip the wreck of food, tools and sailcloth, then learns to grow corn, barley and rice. One ordinary man, surviving, in close-up.

mascot.line: Don't memorize every date. Remember the recipe: new readers, lending libraries, and stories about ordinary lives.

cards.headline: More readers than ever
cards.body: Behind the boom stood readers. From about 1650, a flood of reading matter spread education through the middle classes, especially to women, and that wider readership shows in the rich growth of the prose novel in the 18th century. In England above all, circulating and subscription libraries lent books to members and shaped popular taste, especially in fiction. You no longer had to buy a novel to read one.

cards.headline: A sensation in letters
cards.body: Then came the hits. Samuel Richardson's Pamela (1740), told in letters, follows a servant woman who resists her employer and is rewarded with marriage. It was a publishing sensation, selling in large numbers and provoking parodies, among them Henry Fielding's Shamela (1741). When people start writing parodies of your book, you know it has arrived.

title: Gulliver and the Art of Satire
objective: After this level you can explain why satire uses exaggeration to criticize, using Gulliver's Travels.
summary: Swift's Gulliver's Travels (1726) shrinks real quarrels to egg wars and heel parties in tiny Lilliput. Satire exaggerates what it mocks until the familiar looks absurd.

cards.headline: Eleven thousand people died rather than crack an egg at the wrong end.
cards.body: That's the grim history Gulliver hears in Lilliput, where a law ordered everyone to break their eggs at the smaller end. It is computed, he's told, that "eleven thousand persons" have died rather than obey. Ridiculous? That's exactly the point.

cards.headline: Four strange voyages
cards.body: Jonathan Swift's Gulliver's Travels appeared anonymously in 1726. Its hero sails to Lilliput, where people stand less than 6 inches tall; to Brobdingnag, a land of giants; to Laputa, a flying island; and finally to a land where rational horses, the Houyhnhnms, rule over brutish humanlike creatures, the Yahoos.

cards.headline: Small people, small quarrels
cards.body: Lilliput's egg war mocks the religious quarrels of Swift's day, and its two political parties, told apart by high or low heels, stand for England's Tories and Whigs. The Lilliputians' tiny size mirrors their small-mindedness. Swift doesn't argue that the quarrels are petty. He shrinks them until you can see it for yourself.
cards.callout: Shrink a quarrel, and its pettiness shows.

cards.headline: The trick of satire
cards.body: Satire holds vices and follies up to ridicule, through irony, parody or caricature. The satirist exaggerates what's objectionable, so readers see the absurd in the familiar. Swift even turns it on his own country. After Gulliver proudly describes England, the king of Brobdingnag calls its people "the most pernicious race of little odious vermin that nature ever suffered to crawl upon the surface of the earth."

title: Jane Austen
objective: After this level you can explain why Austen's irony and her way of slipping into a character's thoughts still feel fresh.
summary: Pride and Prejudice (1813) opens with a solemn truth that is really a joke about the marriage market. Austen's free indirect style slips into characters' thoughts, blind spots and all.

cards.headline: Pride and Prejudice opens with a solemn truth. It's a joke.
cards.body: "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife." Now read the next sentence: the neighborhood families consider such a man "the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters." So who, exactly, is in want of whom?

cards.headline: Saying one thing, meaning another
cards.body: Pride and Prejudice was published anonymously in 1813. Its opening runs on irony. Readers have long enjoyed the gap between what the sentence seems to say and the marriage market it really describes, and the drop from its grave start to its comic finish. Austen never explains the joke. She trusts you to catch it.
cards.callout: Irony: the words say one thing; you hear another.

mascot.line: This is Level 52's trick in a new place: a soliloquy lets you hear a mind on stage; this does it on the page.

cards.headline: Inside a head, no quotation marks
cards.body: Austen also made pioneering use of free indirect discourse: third-person narration that takes on a character's own voice, with no "he thought". In Persuasion, the narration slips into Captain Wentworth's view of the woman who once gave him up: "He had not forgiven Anne Elliot. She had used him ill, deserted and disappointed him." Is that the narrator's verdict, or his wounded pride? It's both at once.

cards.headline: Why it still feels fresh
cards.body: Austen could use that inside view to comically undercut a heroine, letting you watch her mistakes from within her own thoughts. Irony keeps you a step ahead of the characters; free indirect style puts you in their heads. She is credited with first giving the novel its distinctly modern character through ordinary people in everyday life. You're not told what to think. You're trusted to notice.

Eighteen had never been printed before, among them Macbeth, The Tempest, As You Like It and Twelfth Night. Without it, Rosalind's disguise and Viola's knot might have been lost forever.

On the page, Austen's narration slipped into a character's voice without a word of speech. Meanwhile prose learned new tricks: Cervantes parodied the romances, Defoe's castaway posed as a real memoir, and Swift's satire held a whole society up to ridicule. And "first recorded in Shakespeare" turned out to mean the earliest written use found so far.

title: The Romantic Poets
objective: After this level you can explain how Wordsworth and Coleridge made nature, feeling and everyday speech the stuff of poetry.
summary: In 1798 Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads, often seen as the start of English Romanticism, put common life, plain speech and powerful feeling into poetry, borrowing the old folk ballad.

cards.headline: In 1798, a slim book of poems with no author's name changed English poetry.
cards.body: It was Lyrical Ballads, by William Wordsworth and Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and it is widely seen as the beginning of the English Romantic movement. Its secret ingredient was surprisingly ordinary.

mascot.line: If you keep one thing from this level: Romantic poems start from ordinary life and plain speech, and they run on feeling.

cards.headline: Poems in the words people really use
cards.body: The book set out to break the polished decorum of Neoclassical verse. Wordsworth's Preface promised "incidents and situations from common life" in "a selection of language really used by men." And the engine was feeling: poetry, he wrote, is "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings" that "takes its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity." First you feel it, later you sit quietly and write it down.

cards.headline: An old folk form, borrowed
cards.body: Why "ballads"? A ballad is a short narrative folk song, re-created from memory at each performance and always changing. Coleridge's poem opened the book with a deliberately old-fashioned title, The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere, and the book's Advertisement admitted it was "professedly written in imitation of the style, as well as of the spirit of the elder poets." The newest poetry in England dressed itself in the oldest clothes.

cards.fact: A sister's journal gave Wordsworth his daffodils.
cards.context: In April 1802 Dorothy Wordsworth described daffodils by Ullswater, in the Lake District, in her journal, and William used her entry for a poem published in 1807. It opens: "I wandered lonely as a Cloud / That floats on high o'er Vales and Hills." Nature seen, feeling recollected, plain words: the Preface in action.

title: The Gothic Novel
objective: After this level you can explain the Gothic toolkit of old castles, buried secrets and dread, from Walpole to Dracula.
summary: The Gothic novel began with Walpole's Castle of Otranto (1764), posed as an old manuscript. Its toolkit of castles, trapdoors, secrets and dread runs through Radcliffe to Stoker's Dracula (1897).

cards.headline: The first Gothic novel opens with a giant helmet crashing down out of nowhere.
cards.body: It crushes the lord's son, Conrad, on his wedding day. That's how Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto begins. Published in 1764, it is generally regarded as the first Gothic novel, and it started a fashion for dread.

cards.headline: A fake old manuscript
cards.body: Walpole didn't sign it. The first edition claimed to be a translation of an old Italian manuscript, printed in Naples in 1529, and only the second edition admitted he'd written it. The genre's name looks backward too: such fiction is called Gothic because its imagination came from medieval buildings and ruins. The past itself was the haunted house.

cards.headline: The toolkit
cards.body: Gothic novels reuse a kit of parts: castles or monasteries with underground passages, dark battlements, hidden panels and trapdoors, all soaked in mystery and terror. Ann Radcliffe, whose The Mysteries of Udolpho (1794) made her England's most popular novelist, added a twist of her own. Her seemingly supernatural events turn out to be natural, but only after a long, delicious wait.

cards.headline: The castle comes to town
cards.body: By 1897 the kit could travel. Bram Stoker's Dracula is told mostly through its characters' own diaries and journals, and its Transylvanian vampire makes his way to England. The Gothic had come home to England.

title: Frankenstein, the Modern Prometheus
objective: After this level you can connect Mary Shelley's Frankenstein to the Prometheus myth and to the birth of science fiction.
summary: Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818), begun in Byron's ghost story contest, swaps Gothic magic for a scientist who makes life. Its subtitle recalls Prometheus, fire-thief and, in Ovid, maker of humans.

cards.headline: A ghost story contest on a stormy summer gave us Frankenstein.
cards.body: In the cold, stormy summer of 1816, near Lake Geneva, Lord Byron challenged his guests to write ghost stories. Mary Shelley came away with something new. In January 1818, aged 20, she published it anonymously: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus.

cards.headline: No ghost, just an experiment
cards.body: Shelley dropped the Gothic's old occult props. Her hero, Victor Frankenstein, is a practicing scientist interested in galvanic electricity, one of the advanced technologies of the early 1800s, and he artificially creates a human being. His creation brings tragedy into his life. The horror isn't a spirit in a castle; it's something a man builds on purpose.

mascot.line: This is Level 7's Ovid again. Old myths keep lending new stories their shape, even a story about science.

cards.headline: Why Prometheus?
cards.body: The subtitle points to an old myth. In Greek myth Prometheus stole fire for humans, and Zeus punished him by fastening him to a mountain. Ovid's Metamorphoses gives him a second job: in one account of the first people, Prometheus mixes new earth with the water of new streams and shapes a man in the image of the gods. A maker of life who pays dearly: that's the frame for Victor.

cards.fact: Frankenstein is often considered an early example of science fiction.
cards.context: It's part Gothic novel and part philosophical novel. But because its what-if rests on an experiment rather than a spell, its champions call Mary Shelley the mother of science fiction.

objective: After this level you can explain how publishing in monthly parts shaped Dickens's cliffhangers, huge casts and fight against poverty.
summary: Dickens published in monthly parts, from Pickwick on, which shaped his many plots and characters and his bond with readers. Oliver Twist attacked the workhouse; from 1858 he read his work aloud.

cards.headline: "Please, sir, I want some more."
cards.body: The starving workhouse boys cast lots over who will ask for more gruel, and it falls to Oliver Twist. He walks up to the master with his basin and says the line above. Dickens's first readers met that scene in a magazine, Bentley's Miscellany, one installment at a time.

cards.headline: A novel by the month
cards.body: Dickens's Pickwick Papers came out in monthly parts in 1836 and 1837. Within a few months it was the rage, and Dickens was the most popular author of the day. He was writing only weeks or days ahead of publication, and he liked the arrangement: later novels repeated Pickwick's pattern of 20 monthly parts.

cards.headline: What the installments did
cards.body: Publishing in parts changed the writing. Each episode had to be shaped on its own, several plots could run side by side, and readers grew unusually close to the author. Dickens filled that space with scores of characters, built from his ear for how people really talk. Think of it as a TV series before television: you came back next month to see what happened.

cards.headline: Aimed at the workhouse
cards.body: Oliver Twist, serialized from 1837 to 1839, is centrally concerned with real social evils: the workhouse and the criminal world. It shows how poverty nurtures crime. That famous bowl of gruel puts the workhouse itself on trial.

cards.fact: From 1858, Dickens read his own work aloud to paying audiences.

summary: Charlotte, Emily and Anne Brontë published as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell to avoid reviewers' treatment of women. Jane Eyre speaks in a fierce first person; Wuthering Heights storms across the moors.

cards.headline: Three new poets: Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell. None of them existed.
cards.body: Their book, Poems, came out in 1846. Behind the names were three sisters: Charlotte, Emily and Anne Brontë.

cards.headline: Why men's names?
cards.body: The sisters wanted secrecy, and they wanted to dodge the special treatment they believed reviewers gave women. Charlotte kept the name Currer Bell for her novels. Her Jane Eyre came out on October 16, 1847, and was an immediate success, far greater than the books her sisters published that same year.

cards.headline: A voice from the inside
cards.body: Jane Eyre is told in the first person by Jane herself, an orphan who becomes a governess and falls in love with her employer, Mr. Rochester. She is a thinking, feeling woman, craving love but able to give it up on principle. When Rochester tries to hold her back, she answers: "I am no bird; and no net ensnares me; I am a free human being with an independent will."

cards.headline: Passion on the moors
cards.body: Emily, as Ellis Bell, published Wuthering Heights in 1847: a highly imaginative novel of passion and hate, set on the Yorkshire moors. Early critics found it too savage, too animal-like and clumsy in construction. Two sisters, two inner storms: one speaks straight to you, the other howls across the heather.

title: Realism: Life as It Is
objective: After this level you can explain how realist novelists like Flaubert and George Eliot made ordinary lives the subject of serious art.
summary: Realism depicted ordinary life without embellishment. Flaubert's Madame Bovary, told with cool objectivity, put him on trial in 1857; George Eliot preferred an old woman at her flower-pot to angels.

cards.headline: In 1857, France put a novel on trial.
cards.body: Madame Bovary had just run in installments, and the government tried Gustave Flaubert for its alleged immorality. He narrowly escaped conviction. The book's subtitle sounds harmless enough: Provincial Customs.

cards.headline: A woman who read too many romances
cards.body: Emma Bovary destroys herself trying to base her life on the passion and happiness she found in popular romance novels. Flaubert tells it with unrelenting objectivity, recording every trait and incident without comment. He spent about five years on the book, hunting for "le seul mot juste," the one right word.

cards.headline: What realism means
cards.body: That's realism: the accurate, detailed, unembellished picture of contemporary life. Realists wrote about the middle and lower classes, the unexceptional and the ordinary. Between 1850 and 1880 it was a major trend in French novels and paintings. No knights, no ghosts, no dragons: the drama is in everyday life.

cards.headline: An old woman instead of angels
cards.body: In England, Mary Ann Evans wrote as George Eliot. In Adam Bede she stops the story to praise Dutch paintings for their "faithful pictures of a monotonous homely existence." She turns, she says, "from cloud-borne angels, from prophets, sibyls, and heroic warriors, to an old woman bending over her flower-pot." Her Middlemarch is subtitled A Study of Provincial Life.

title: Tolstoy's Big Canvas
objective: After this level you can explain how War and Peace and Anna Karenina weave private lives into the history around them.
summary: Tolstoy's War and Peace sets fictional families inside Napoleon's 1812 invasion and denies that great men make history. Anna Karenina sets Anna's doomed affair against a hypocritical society.

cards.headline: One book opens on unhappy families, the other on the eve of a war.
cards.body: Anna Karenina begins, in Constance Garnett's translation: "Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way." Leo Tolstoy's earlier War and Peace starts in St. Petersburg in 1805 and heads for Napoleon's invasion. Both are about private lives inside a bigger story.

cards.headline: History with people in it
cards.body: War and Peace (1865 to 1869) centers on the French invasion of Russia in 1812. It mixes three things: a history of the Napoleonic Wars, the lives of fictional characters such as Pierre Bezukhov, Prince Andrey Bolkonsky and the Rostov family, and essays on the philosophy of history. A battle and a family dinner share the same pages.

mascot.line: This is Level 1's line between epic and novel, drawn inside one book: heroic deeds shrink, ordinary lives grow.

cards.headline: No great men
cards.body: Those essays make a bold claim. Tolstoy rejects the idea that history is shaped by great men and stresses the part ordinary people play. Napoleon's invasion is the backdrop, but no single great man steers events. The weight falls on countless lives like Pierre's.

cards.headline: Anna's private war
cards.body: Anna Karenina, published in installments between 1875 and 1877, centers on Anna's affair with Count Vronsky. Alongside it runs the courtship and marriage of Kitty and Levin, a counterpoint to Anna's tragedy. Anna pays not so much for breaking the moral code as for refusing the proprieties her hypocritical high society expects. The society around her is part of the plot.

title: Dostoevsky's Crime and Punishment
objective: After this level you can explain how Crime and Punishment turns a murder into a psychological drama of guilt and conscience.
summary: In Dostoyevsky's Crime and Punishment (1866), a poor student kills a pawnbroker to prove a theory. The real drama is his guilt: Porfiry's mind games, Sonya's persuasion, confession and Siberia.

cards.headline: A poor student kills an old pawnbroker. Then the real story starts.
cards.body: Fyodor Dostoyevsky's Crime and Punishment, first published in 1866, follows what comes after the crime: Raskolnikov's descent into psychological torment.

cards.headline: A theory that permits a crime
cards.body: Raskolnikov, an impoverished former student in St. Petersburg, decides to solve his problems at a stroke by murdering an old pawnbroker. He has a theory to back it: extraordinary people must have "the right to transgress," or progress would be impossible. The rest of the book puts that theory on trial, inside his own head.

cards.headline: Cat and mouse
cards.body: The detective Porfiry Petrovich guesses who did it but can't prove it, so he plays psychological games instead. Raskolnikov does half the work for him: conscience and mounting suspicion wear him down. The chase happens in conversations, not in alleys. You know who did it from the start; the suspense is whether he will crack.

cards.headline: Confession and Siberia
cards.body: His way out comes through Sonya. She persuades Raskolnikov to confess, and she follows him to Siberia. Even there he clings at first to his theories; repentance comes slowly. By the end, the punishment in the title means much more than a prison sentence.

title: Ibsen, Chekhov and the Modern Stage
objective: After this level you can explain how Ibsen and Chekhov brought ordinary homes and unresolved endings to the stage.
summary: Ibsen's A Doll's House (1879) put a realistic middle-class marriage on stage and ends with Nora slamming the door. Chekhov moved the big events offstage; The Cherry Orchard ends with distant axes.

cards.headline: A wife walks out, the door slams, and the play just ends.
cards.body: That's the final moment of Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House (1879). Nora declares her independence and leaves her husband and children, slamming the door of the house behind her. What happens to her next, the play never shows.

cards.headline: Drama in the living room
cards.body: Ibsen set his moral questions against a severely realistic middle-class background. Nora once secretly forged a signature to get the money that saved her husband Torvald's life. When the secret comes out, he turns on her to protect his reputation. No kings, no battles: a loan, a marriage and a front door.

cards.headline: Chekhov turns the volume down
cards.body: Anton Chekhov went quieter still. His plays about the day-to-day life of Russia's landowning families achieved a delicate poetic realism, and most of their climactic action happens offstage: you watch people react. The Seagull was badly received in 1896, then succeeded when the new Moscow Art Theatre staged it in 1898.

cards.headline: The sound of axes
cards.body: In The Cherry Orchard (1904) a family's estate is sold to pay its debts, and the merchant Lopakhin buys it. The play ends with axes heard offstage, cutting down the orchard. Chekhov called it a comedy. Is it? Like Nora's slammed door, the ending leaves that question with you.

title: Poe and the Short Story
objective: After this level you can explain Poe's idea that a short story should build toward a single effect.
summary: Poe's 1842 review of Hawthorne argued a tale should be read in one sitting and built backward from a single effect; he later claimed he wrote The Raven like a math problem.

cards.headline: Poe had a rule: a story should fit in one sitting.
cards.body: In May 1842, Edgar Allan Poe reviewed Nathaniel Hawthorne's Twice-Told Tales in Graham's Magazine and used it to set out a theory. The best prose tale, he said, is short, "requiring from a half-hour to one or two hours in its perusal". Why should the length of a story matter so much?

mascot.line: If you remember one thing from this level: Poe starts from the effect on you and works backward to the story.

cards.headline: Start with the feeling, then build the story
cards.body: Poe's recipe runs backward. A skilful writer first decides on "a certain unique or single effect", the feeling the reader should be left with. Only then does he invent the incidents that bring it about, and no word may drift from that one design. Poe's strictest line: "If his very initial sentence tend not to the outbringing of this effect, then he has failed in his first step." Dread, grief, suspense: pick one, and aim everything at it.
cards.callout: The single effect: choose the feeling first, then build every part to deliver it.

cards.headline: Why a novel can't do it
cards.body: Here's where length comes in. A novel, Poe argued, "cannot be read at one sitting", so it loses "the immense force derivable from totality". You put the book down, the rest of your life walks in, and the spell weakens. A tale you finish in one go keeps its whole effect intact. Think of a song heard straight through versus one interrupted by a string of phone calls.

cards.fact: Poe claimed he built "The Raven" like a math problem.
cards.context: In "The Philosophy of Composition" (1846), Poe said the poem proceeded step by step "with the precision and rigid consequence of a mathematical problem". First he chose a melancholy tone; then he picked the refrain "Nevermore" to fit it. Whether or not he really worked that coolly, the method stuck. Many anthologies now credit Poe as the "architect" of the modern short story.

title: The Scarlet Letter
objective: After this level you can explain how Hawthorne used a symbol to judge the Puritan past.
summary: In The Scarlet Letter (1850), Hester Prynne must wear an A for adultery in Puritan Boston, yet the town comes to say it means Able. Hawthorne, a Salem judge's descendant, judges the Puritan past.

cards.headline: Hawthorne claimed he found the scarlet A in a dusty government office.
cards.body: The Scarlet Letter opens with a trick. Hawthorne had worked at the Salem Custom House, and in the novel's introduction he describes it and pretends to find the story among an old surveyor's papers. With them lies a faded rag of scarlet cloth shaped like the capital letter A. The novel sets out to explain it.

cards.headline: A letter you have to wear
cards.body: The story goes back to the Puritans of 17th-century Boston. Hester Prynne has had a child outside marriage, and her punishment is to wear a scarlet A, for adultery, on her dress where everyone can see it. When she is ordered to name the child's father, she refuses. The town means the letter to fix her identity in a single word.

cards.headline: The letter changes its meaning
cards.body: Hester's A is no plain patch: it is fine red cloth "surrounded with an elaborate embroidery and fantastic flourishes of gold-thread". Then, through years of helping her neighbors, something shifts. Many people refuse to read the A in its first sense: "They said that it meant Able; so strong was Hester Prynne, with a woman's strength." The town made the symbol, and the town ends up changing what it says.

cards.fact: Hawthorne's own ancestor questioned accused witches at Salem.
cards.context: John Hathorne was a magistrate and the stern interrogator of the accused in the Salem witch trials. Hawthorne was haunted by such ancestors, and they turn up in his fiction. In the introduction he writes that he takes "shame upon myself for their sakes". So when the novel judges Puritan harshness, a descendant is judging his own family.

title: Moby-Dick
objective: After this level you can explain how Melville turned a whaling voyage into an epic of obsession.
summary: Melville turned his whaling years and the wreck of the Essex into Moby-Dick (1851): Captain Ahab's revenge hunt for the white whale, an epic novel that flopped and was rediscovered in the 1920s.

cards.headline: "Call me Ishmael." Then a whaling voyage turns into something much bigger.
cards.body: Herman Melville knew whaling firsthand. In January 1841, at 21, he sailed out of New Bedford harbor on the whaleship Acushnet. His narrator, Ishmael, later calls a whale ship "my Yale College and my Harvard". Moby-Dick (1851) starts out as a sailor's story. It doesn't stay one.

cards.headline: One captain, one passion
cards.body: The Pequod's captain, Ahab, has lost a leg to a white whale called Moby Dick. He tells his crew plainly: "it was Moby Dick that dismasted me". From then on the voyage bends toward a single target. Ishmael says Ahab "seemed ready to sacrifice all mortal interests to that one passion". A business trip for whale oil has become a revenge quest, and the whole crew is aboard for it.

mascot.line: People mix these up. An epic is a poem. Moby-Dick borrows the epic's size, but in prose, so it is still a novel.

cards.headline: An epic, in prose
cards.body: Level 1 drew the line: an epic is a long narrative poem of heroic deeds, while a novel is an invented story in prose. Moby-Dick is a novel, yet it is often called Melville's "epic novel", and it has the scale: a towering captain, a doomed quest, an ocean-sized stage. Hawthorne is widely credited with inspiring Melville to turn early drafts of a sea adventure into this huge book, and Melville dedicated it to him.

cards.fact: The whale wins.
cards.context: In the final chase Ahab cries "from hell's heart I stab at thee", the whale destroys the Pequod, and only Ishmael survives to tell it. Real life supplied the shape: in 1820 a sperm whale rammed and sank the whaleship Essex, a story Melville first heard aboard the Acushnet. Moby-Dick flopped with critics and buyers and was not rediscovered until the 1920s.

title: Douglass's Narrative
objective: After this level you can explain how Frederick Douglass's 1845 Narrative made reading and writing the road to freedom.
summary: Douglass's 1845 Narrative shows how a banned reading lesson taught him that literacy was the pathway from slavery to freedom, and how he learned in secret and wrote the book himself.

cards.headline: A banned alphabet lesson taught a boy the most important thing.
cards.body: In Baltimore, the enslaved boy Frederick Douglass lived in the Auld household. Sophia Auld "very kindly commenced to teach me the A, B, C", he later wrote, then helped him spell short words. Her husband found out and forbade it. Reading, Mr. Auld said, "would forever unfit him to be a slave".

cards.headline: The ban was the clue
cards.body: Auld meant to shut a door. Instead he showed Douglass where the door was. If reading would unfit a person for slavery, then reading was a way out. "From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom," Douglass wrote. He had gained that lesson, he said, by accident, from the very master who banned the others.

cards.headline: Bread for lessons
cards.body: So Douglass kept learning in secret. He made friends with the white boys he met in the street and turned them into teachers, giving them bread in return for what he called "that more valuable bread of knowledge". He learned to write from the letters ship carpenters marked on timber: L for larboard, S for starboard. At twelve he got The Columbian Orator, a book of speeches and writings on natural rights.

cards.fact: The title ends with three words: "Written by Himself."
cards.context: Douglass escaped slavery in 1838, disguised as a sailor, and became a famous speaker. Some audiences suspected he had never been enslaved at all. So in 1845 he published his Narrative, full of real names and places, to lay those doubts to rest. The title page makes the point on its own: the boy once forbidden the alphabet wrote the book.

title: Whitman's Leaves of Grass
objective: After this level you can explain how Whitman's long free-verse lines tried to hold all of America.
summary: Whitman self-published twelve untitled poems in 1855. His 'I' grows to hold every reader, his long free-verse catalogs list working Americans, and he kept expanding the book until he died.

cards.headline: In 1855 a Brooklyn printer published a book of twelve untitled poems.
cards.body: Walt Whitman had worked in Brooklyn as a printer and newspaper journalist. The first Leaves of Grass was a slim book he published himself: twelve poems with no titles, plus a preface. Inside was a voice that wanted to hold an entire country.

cards.headline: "I" means you too
cards.body: The poem later famous as "Song of Myself" opens: "I celebrate myself, and sing myself, / And what I assume you shall assume, / For every atom belonging to me as good belongs to you." Whitman's "myself" keeps swelling until it takes in the reader, then everyone. Caught contradicting himself, he shrugs: "Very well then I contradict myself, / (I am large, I contain multitudes.)"

cards.headline: A list as long as a country
cards.body: One of Whitman's great tools is the list. In "I Hear America Singing" come the mechanics, the carpenter, the mason, the boatman, the shoemaker, "Each singing what belongs to him or her and to none else". The lines run long, with no rhyme and no regular beat: what the National Park Service calls "a free-verse avalanche". A country that big needed a line that long.

cards.fact: Whitman spent the rest of his life rewriting one book.
cards.context: He kept refining Leaves of Grass through edition after edition. The second, in 1856, already had thirty-two poems. The last, the "deathbed edition" of 1891-92, was finished only weeks before he died in 1892. Like the singers of Homer's tradition, who reshaped inherited poems in every performance, Whitman kept reshaping his book for nearly four decades.

title: Emily Dickinson
objective: After this level you can explain how Dickinson packed large ideas into short poems with slant rhyme and dashes.
summary: Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems, barely any published in her life. She packed death and hope into hymn-sized common meter with slant rhyme; early editors removed her dashes.

cards.headline: When she died, her family found nearly 1,800 poems almost no one had read.
cards.body: Emily Dickinson composed almost 1,800 poems, but fewer than a dozen were published in her lifetime. After she died in 1886, her family discovered forty little booklets she had made herself, folding and sewing sheets of stationery and copying her poems inside. A whole life's work, bound by hand and waiting.

cards.headline: Hymn-sized poems, enormous subjects
cards.body: Dickinson often wrote in common meter: lines of eight and six syllables, taking turns, the beat of hymns like "Amazing Grace". Into that small, familiar box she packed the largest subjects there are. Here is death, as the 1890s editions print it, arriving like a polite caller: "Because I could not stop for Death, / He kindly stopped for me; / The carriage held but just ourselves / And Immortality."

cards.headline: Rhymes that land slightly off
cards.body: Listen to the line endings. "Me" and "Immortality" nearly rhyme, but not quite. So do "soul" and "all" in "Hope is the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul, / And sings the tune without the words, / And never stops at all,". That near miss is slant rhyme, rhyme that isn't perfect, and the poets of her day used it far less often. The sound never quite settles, and neither do the ideas.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the editions. Just remember: the quotes here are the tidied 1890s text, not her own dashing handwriting.

cards.context: Dickinson punctuated mostly with dashes; in her handwriting they come in many sizes and directions, some even vertical. The first printed books, from 1890, followed the editors' taste and removed her marks, which is why the lines quoted here look so tidy. Today's standard edition prints her dashes as en dashes, closer to what she wrote.

title: Huckleberry Finn
objective: After this level you can explain why Twain's novel told in a boy's own voice changed American writing and still sparks debate.
summary: Twain let Huck narrate a whole novel in his own speech, a break writers such as Hemingway saw as the start of modern American writing. Huck's choice to help Jim anchors a still-live debate.

cards.headline: This novel opens by threatening to shoot anyone who looks for a plot.
cards.body: Before the story of Adventures of Huckleberry Finn begins, Mark Twain posts a notice: "persons attempting to find a moral in it will be banished; persons attempting to find a plot in it will be shot." It's a joke, and a warning: this book won't sound like a lesson.

cards.headline: A boy tells it his way
cards.body: Then Huck starts talking: "You don't know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that ain't no matter." The whole novel stays in his voice. Critic Tony Tanner called that revolutionary: earlier books let rough-spoken characters talk, but always inside a polished adult narrator's frame. Here the boy owns the book. Ernest Hemingway later declared that all modern American literature comes from it.

cards.headline: The wrong reason to do the right thing
cards.body: Huck, a poor white boy, befriends Jim, a man who has escaped slavery. Huck has been taught that helping Jim is a sin. He writes a letter that would betray Jim, then tears it up: "All right, then, I'll go to hell." He believes he is damning himself by doing right. Defenders read the book as satire, and this is their evidence: the joke is on a society whose idea of sin is upside down.

cards.headline: Still argued over
cards.body: The arguments began early: soon after publication, the book was banned in Concord, Massachusetts. Today they turn on race. Critics point to its repeated racial slur and a portrayal of Jim along minstrel-show lines; in 2000 the Pennsylvania NAACP and professor Jonathan Arac wanted it off required reading lists. Defenders such as scholar Jocelyn Chadwick argue for teaching it as satire of racism. Satire or Evasion? (1992), essays by African American scholars, spans the whole range.

title: The Harlem Renaissance
objective: After this level you can explain how Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston brought Black speech and music into American literature.

cards.headline: A poem that sways like a blues piano.
cards.body: "Droning a drowsy syncopated tune, / Rocking back and forth to a mellow croon," So begins "The Weary Blues", the title poem of Langston Hughes's first book, published in 1926. Hughes became a fixture of the Harlem Renaissance, the 1920s flowering that celebrated African American culture and achievement. His idea: let the poem move like the music.

cards.headline: The blues on the page
cards.body: Hughes said the people he met were the influences of his work, but blues and jazz were its rhythm. He wanted to tell his people's stories the way they actually lived them, with their music, laughter and language. Among his main influences he named Walt Whitman. You met Whitman's long, crowded lines in Level 75; Hughes filled that American song with Black voices.

cards.headline: An anthropologist on her own front porch
cards.body: Zora Neale Hurston grew up in Eatonville, Florida, incorporated in 1887 as one of the nation's first Black towns. On the porch of the village store, she heard people spin colorful stories. At Barnard College she studied anthropology with Franz Boas, then went home to Florida to collect folklore. The result, Mules and Men (1935), put Black Southern folklore in print.

cards.fact: In her great novel, every character talks the way the rural South talked.

title: Toni Morrison's Beloved
objective: After this level you can explain how Morrison's Beloved turns the history of slavery into a story about memory.
summary: Morrison's Beloved (1987) grew from the 1856 case of Margaret Garner. It changes the history, tells it from the inside, and breaks time into pieces so the past moves back into the house.

cards.headline: The house at 124 Bluestone Road is haunted, and everyone knows it.
cards.body: Toni Morrison's Beloved (1987) opens in Cincinnati in 1873. In Sethe's house, chairs move by themselves, kettles turn over and handprints appear in cake icing. Sethe, who escaped slavery, believes the ghost is her older daughter, who died before she was two. Why would a mother's home be haunted by her own child?

cards.headline: A true case from 1856
cards.body: The seed is history. In 1856 Margaret Garner, an enslaved woman who had escaped to Cincinnati, was about to be forced back to Kentucky under fugitive slave laws. She killed her infant daughter rather than see the child returned to slavery. The law charged her not with murder but with destroying her owner's property. Morrison came across the case in an 1856 newspaper clipping while compiling The Black Book (1974).

cards.headline: Fiction that answers the record
cards.body: Beloved is not a retelling. Morrison changes the ending: Sethe and her daughter Denver finish the novel alive and free, while the real Margaret Garner was recaptured and died in captivity. Morrison said that telling the story through the characters' inner lives puts authority back in the hands of the enslaved, not the slaveholder. The court record treated a child as property; the novel treats every one of its people as a person.

cards.headline: A past that walks in the door
cards.body: Then a mysterious young woman named Beloved appears, the age Sethe's dead daughter would have been, and Sethe takes her in. The book jumps between its present after the Civil War and flashbacks from before Emancipation, the way painful memory surfaces: in pieces, out of order. Its characters work every day at beating back the past. In Beloved, the past doesn't stay buried. It moves in.

title: Modernism: Make It New
objective: After this level you can explain why writers after World War I broke with traditional plots and forms.
summary: After World War I shook faith in Western culture, modernists broke old forms. Pound's slogan was Make It New; Joyce's Ulysses (1922) turned Homer's Odyssey into one ordinary Dublin day.

cards.headline: Modernism came to be summed up as "Make it new." The phrase itself was ancient.
cards.body: Ezra Pound used Make It New as the title of a 1934 book of essays, and decades later it became the label for modernist newness. He took it from a Chinese anecdote: Tang, first king of the Shang dynasty, was said to have had the words inscribed on his washbasin. So what were modern writers trying to make new, and why then?

cards.headline: A war that broke the old forms
cards.body: Modernism was a period of experiment in the arts, running from the late 19th to the mid-20th century. As a literary movement, though, it belongs above all to the years after World War I (1914 to 1918). The war's sheer enormity undermined faith in the foundations of Western society and culture, and postwar writing filled with disillusionment and fragmentation. If the world had broken into pieces, why should a story arrive in one neat piece?

cards.headline: What they broke
cards.body: Modernist writers challenged the conventions not just of their parents' day but of the whole post-Romantic era. Their experiments were radical. Stream of consciousness followed the flow of a mind instead of a tidy plot. Poems were assembled from fragmentary images and allusions. And readers were expected to take an active role in working out what it all meant. The story no longer came with a tour guide.

cards.headline: 1922: an ordinary day as an epic
cards.body: The landmark year was 1922, when both T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land and James Joyce's Ulysses appeared. Ulysses, first published in Paris, follows three Dubliners through a single day, June 16, 1904. It runs parallel to Homer's Odyssey: Leopold Bloom is Odysseus, Stephen Dedalus is Telemachus, and Molly Bloom is Penelope. The point: an ordinary modern life deserves the same attention as a hero's.

title: Poems from the Trenches
objective: After this level you can weigh how war poets like Wilfred Owen answered the old idea that dying for your country is sweet.
summary: Horace said dying for your country is sweet and fitting. Rupert Brooke's 1914 sonnets kept that idealism; Wilfred Owen, after a gas attack, called it "the old Lie."

cards.headline: A Roman poet said dying for your country is sweet. A soldier disagreed.
cards.body: The Roman poet Horace put it in his Odes: Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori, "it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country." In World War I, two young British poets answered that line in opposite ways. Which answer should you trust?

cards.headline: Brooke: a corner of a foreign field
cards.body: Rupert Brooke's war sonnets, published as 1914 and Other Poems in 1915, made him famous overnight. They face death with idealism. "The Soldier" begins: "If I should die, think only this of me: / That there's some corner of a foreign field / That is for ever England." Brooke died of blood poisoning on a hospital ship off Skyros on April 23, 1915, on his way to the Dardanelles.

cards.headline: Owen: "The old Lie"
cards.body: Wilfred Owen drafted "Dulce et Decorum Est" in 1917 at Craiglockhart War Hospital, where he was being treated for shell shock. It describes a gas attack like one he had lived through. It opens on exhausted soldiers, "Bent double, like old beggars under sacks," and ends by naming Horace's line "The old Lie." Britannica sets Brooke's idealism in strong contrast to this later poetry of the trenches.

cards.headline: The Poetry is in the pity
cards.body: Few of Owen's poems were printed in his lifetime. He was killed on November 4, 1918, leading his men across the Sambre-Oise canal, and his parents got the news on November 11, Armistice Day. His Poems appeared in 1920. The preface begins: "This book is not about heroes." A few lines on: "The Poetry is in the pity."

title: The Waste Land
objective: After this level you can explain how T. S. Eliot built a poem from fragments and borrowed voices, and why readers found it hard.
summary: Eliot's The Waste Land (1922) runs 433 lines of fragments, allusions and other languages, tied together by Tiresias from Ovid. Pound cut it; Eliot's notes admit its difficulty.

cards.headline: "April is the cruellest month." A poem that turns spring upside down.
cards.body: That's the opening of T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land, which first appeared in 1922, in The Criterion in London and then The Dial in New York. Spring usually means new life. Here it hurts. And the rest of the poem arrives in pieces. How do you build a poem out of fragments?

cards.headline: A poem made of pieces
cards.body: The Waste Land is a 433-line poem in five parts. It weaves in allusions to Chaucer, Dante, Shakespeare, classical myth, the Bible and the Upanishads, and it ends in Sanskrit: "Shantih shantih shantih," which Eliot's note calls a formal ending to an Upanishad. Near that end, one line describes the whole method: "These fragments I have shored against my ruins." The poem tells you how it was built.

cards.headline: Borrowed voices, Ovid's among them
cards.body: The book edition added Eliot's own notes. One names Tiresias, the blind seer of Greek myth, as the most important personage, uniting all the rest: "What Tiresias sees, in fact, is the substance of the poem." The note then quotes Ovid's Latin about Tiresias, and another sends readers to Ovid's Metamorphoses for Philomela. The voices are many, but one old seer holds them together.

cards.headline: Hard on purpose?
cards.body: Ezra Pound helped cut the original manuscript to nearly half its size, which made it denser still. Critics split: its complex, learned style was denounced for obscurity and praised for its Modernism. Even Eliot's first note admits the problem, saying Jessie L. Weston's book on the Grail legend "will elucidate the difficulties of the poem much better than my notes can do." The poem expects you to bring a library.

title: Stream of Consciousness
objective: After this level you can explain how Joyce and Woolf put a character's flowing thoughts on the page.
summary: Stream of consciousness, a phrase from William James, follows thoughts as they flow. Joyce ends Ulysses in Molly Bloom's mind; Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway slips between minds in one London day.

cards.headline: A novel that ends inside a mind: "yes I said yes I will Yes."
cards.body: Those are the last words of James Joyce's Ulysses (1922). They close Molly Bloom's monologue, her thoughts set down directly in her own voice, as if the author had stepped out of the room. How do you put the flow of a mind on paper?

cards.headline: A psychologist's phrase
cards.body: The psychologist William James used the phrase stream of consciousness in The Principles of Psychology (1890). In fiction it names a technique that tries to render the flow of impressions passing through one person's mind: sights, sounds, feelings, associations. It commonly ignores orderly sentence structure and lets fragments of thought through. Nobody thinks in tidy paragraphs.

cards.headline: Woolf's day in London
cards.body: Virginia Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway (1925) follows Clarissa Dalloway through one day in London as she prepares a party. It opens plainly: "Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself." A moment later, a squeak of hinges she can hear now carries her back to Bourton, when she was a girl of eighteen. One small sound, and the past floods in.

cards.headline: From mind to mind
cards.body: Woolf's narration moves fluidly between characters' thoughts: from Clarissa to Septimus Warren Smith, a World War I veteran with shell shock. She was influenced by Joyce's Ulysses. Big Ben marks the day's hours, and again and again as it strikes, one phrase returns: "The leaden circles dissolved in the air." The clock keeps public time while the minds wander.

mascot.line: People mix these two up. Every stream of consciousness is inner, but not every interior monologue is a stream.

cards.headline: Not quite the same thing
cards.body: Interior monologue is often used as another name for stream of consciousness. But an interior monologue can be limited to a character's organized, rational thoughts. The stream lets in everything: every half thought, impression and stray association.

title: Kafka's Metamorphosis
objective: After this level you can weigh two readings of Kafka's story of a man who wakes up as an insect.
summary: In Kafka's Die Verwandlung (1915), Gregor Samsa wakes as a monstrous vermin and worries about work. Readers weigh two readings: a family story and a story about dehumanizing labor.

cards.headline: A salesman wakes up as a giant insect. His first worry? Being late.
cards.body: Franz Kafka's story, first published in German in 1915, opens with Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, changed in his bed into a gigantic insect. Before panic, before horror, his mind goes to work and his demanding boss. What kind of story starts like that?

cards.headline: Changed, but into what?
cards.body: Kafka called it Die Verwandlung, "the transformation." He had translated part of Ovid's Metamorphoses at school, yet he didn't borrow Ovid's title. His first sentence calls Gregor an "ungeheueren Ungeziefer", roughly a monstrous vermin, and he kept the creature's exact kind vague. He even told his publisher the insect must not be drawn on the cover, not even from a distance.

cards.headline: Reading 1: the family
cards.body: Gregor is his family's sole provider. Once he changes, their response moves from shock to rejection, and his sister, who first cares for him, finally insists they must get rid of the monster. Kafka's own father was a domineering businessman. In 1919 Kafka wrote him a long letter he never sent, and Britannica says it reveals the background to the father-son conflict in many of his stories.

mascot.line: You don't have to pick one reading. Ask which clues each one explains best, then weigh them.

cards.headline: Reading 2: the job
cards.body: Look at what Gregor thinks about first. He frets that he has missed the five o'clock train, and the next leaves at seven. Scholars read the story through several lenses, and one is the dehumanizing effects of labor. title: Gatsby and the Lost Generation
objective: After this level you can weigh what The Great Gatsby says about the American Dream.
summary: Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby (1925): a self-made man reaches for Daisy's green light and the past. Is the dream the problem, or the "foul dust" around it? Readers weigh both.

cards.headline: Across the bay from a mansion, a green light burns all night.
cards.body: It sits at the end of Daisy's dock in F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby (1925), a novel narrated by Nick Carraway. "You always have a green light that burns all night at the end of your dock," Gatsby tells her. What is he reaching for, and what does the book think of it?

cards.headline: The self-made man
cards.body: Jay Gatsby is a self-made millionaire from humble roots, born James Gatz, who grew rich bootlegging during Prohibition. He pursues Daisy Buchanan, whom he loved in his youth, though she has married Tom. When Nick warns, "You can't repeat the past," Gatsby answers: "Can't repeat the past? Why of course you can!" He wants the money, the girl and the lost years back.

cards.headline: Reading 1: a dream gone sour
cards.body: Britannica reads the novel as a pessimistic examination of the American Dream, showing how materialism corrupts ambition. The green light stands for Gatsby's unattainable dream. The book's last line leans the same way: "So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past."

cards.headline: Reading 2: a gift for hope
cards.body: Yet Nick admires him. He praises Gatsby's "extraordinary gift for hope, a romantic readiness such as I have never found in any other person." And he insists Gatsby "turned out all right at the end"; what preyed on him was the "foul dust" that floated in the wake of his dreams. So is the dream the problem, or the world around it?

cards.headline: A lost generation
cards.body: Fitzgerald belonged to the Lost Generation: American writers who came of age in World War I and made their names in the 1920s, disillusioned with postwar society. The name is credited to Gertrude Stein, and Hemingway put her remark, "You are all a lost generation," at the front of The Sun Also Rises (1926). Gatsby was not a commercial success in 1925. It is now a classic.

title: Tagore and Gitanjali
objective: After this level you can explain how Rabindranath Tagore's songs became the first Nobel-winning work by a writer from outside Europe.
summary: Tagore's Bengali songs, sung wherever Bengali is spoken, became Gitanjali (1912) in his own English prose. In 1913 he became the first non-European Nobel laureate in literature.

cards.headline: In 1913 the Nobel Prize in Literature left Europe for the first time.
cards.body: It went to Rabindranath Tagore, a Bengali poet, and above all for a slim book of religious songs he had put into English prose himself. How did songs from Bengal become a prize-winning book in the West?

cards.headline: Song offerings
cards.body: The English Gitanjali (1912) is subtitled Song Offerings. It gathers Tagore's own prose translations of religious poems from several of his Bengali collections, with an introduction by the Irish poet W. B. Yeats. Poem 35 begins: "Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high;". In English they read as prose poems. In Bengal they were songs.

cards.headline: Songs before they were a book
cards.body: Tagore composed more than 2,000 songs, popular among all classes of Bengali society, and the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh are his. Yeats's introduction reports a Bengali doctor telling him the songs "are sung from the west of India into Burma wherever Bengali is spoken," and says Tagore "writes music for his words." This was poetry people carried in their voices.

cards.headline: In his own English words
cards.body: The 1913 prize motivation praises verse "by which, with consummate skill, he has made his poetic thought, expressed in his own English words, a part of the literature of the West." Yeats admitted what English readers missed: the Bengali originals, he was told, were full of "untranslatable delicacies of colour." The prize-winning book was the poet translating himself.

title: Things Fall Apart
objective: After this level you can explain how Chinua Achebe wrote back against colonial stories about Africa.
summary: Achebe's Things Fall Apart (1958) tells an Igbo story from the inside, in English peppered with Igbo proverbs, to answer colonial novels that cast Africa's past as savagery.

cards.headline: A novel ends with an official planning a book. Its hero gets a paragraph.
cards.body: On the last page of Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart, the District Commissioner decides Okonkwo's story might fill a paragraph in his planned book, The Pacification of the Primitive Tribes of the Lower Niger. Achebe had just given Okonkwo an entire novel. That gap is the point.

cards.headline: Inside an Igbo village
cards.body: Things Fall Apart, written in English and published in 1958, follows Okonkwo, a leader of an Igbo community, as white missionaries and colonial government intrude in the 1890s. It is traditionally structured and peppered with Igbo proverbs, and it traces the falling apart of Okonkwo and of his village at the same time. You see the world before you see it break.

mascot.line: Keep this: Achebe wasn't only telling a story. He was correcting one that others had told.

cards.headline: Why Achebe wrote it
cards.body: Achebe resented the stereotype of Africa as a primitive land, a "heart of darkness," and novels like Joyce Cary's Mister Johnson, with its comic African who adores his white boss. In his essay "The Novelist as Teacher", he said he'd be satisfied if his novels about the past taught readers one thing: their past, imperfect as it was, had not been an age of savagery from which Europeans rescued them.

cards.headline: A title from Yeats
cards.body: Achebe took his title from W. B. Yeats's poem "The Second Coming": "Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold;". An Igbo story, told in English under an Irish poet's line, answers the colonial novel in its own language. Britannica credits the book with helping create the Nigerian literary renaissance of the 1960s.

title: Magical Realism
objective: After this level you can explain how magical realism treats the impossible as ordinary, from Gabriel García Márquez's Macondo onward.
summary: Magical realism states the impossible as plain fact. In García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967), Remedios rises to heaven while hanging sheets, and nobody is much surprised.

cards.headline: A young woman rises into heaven while hanging out the sheets.
cards.body: It happens in Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude: Remedios the Beauty ascends one day while hanging sheets to dry. In this novel, magic rarely earns surprise. How can a book make the impossible feel ordinary?

cards.headline: Magic, stated plainly
cards.body: Magic realism is the matter-of-fact inclusion of fantastic or mythical elements in otherwise realistic fiction. It's linked above all with Latin American writers: García Márquez, Jorge Luis Borges, Julio Cortázar, Isabel Allende. The term began in painting. The German critic Franz Roh coined it in 1925 for realist paintings with fantasy or dreamlike subjects.

cards.headline: Welcome to Macondo
cards.body: One Hundred Years of Solitude (Cien años de soledad), published in Spanish in 1967, follows seven generations of the Buendía family in Macondo, a fictional Colombian town based on García Márquez's hometown, Aracataca. It rains for four years, eleven months and two days. Yellow butterflies always accompany one young man, Mauricio Babilonia. The world is real, and so is the magic.

cards.headline: Grandmother's straight face
cards.body: García Márquez said his grandmother told fantastic, supernatural stories without ever changing her expression. To write the novel, he found he had to believe the stories himself and tell them the same way. That deadpan tone is the trick. Tell a miracle the way you'd mention the weather, and the reader nods along.
