title: Fairy Tales Written Down
objective: After this level you can compare versions of a fairy tale by Perrault, the Grimms and Andersen and explain why they differ.
summary: Perrault's Cinderella (1697) has a glass slipper and forgives her stepsisters; the Grimms', from oral sources, blinds them; Andersen invented his own tales.

cards.headline: The glass slipper? Only one Cinderella wears it.
cards.body: You probably picture Cinderella in glass slippers. But the glass slipper is unique to one version, Charles Perrault's. In other tellings the token is often a golden or silver slipper, or a ring. Same story, different details. So why would tellers change a story everyone knows?

cards.headline: Perrault's polite Cinderella
cards.body: Perrault's Cinderella appeared in 1697 in his Tales of Mother Goose: modern versions of half-forgotten folk tales, retold in a simple style and written to amuse his children. A fairy godmother gives her the glass slippers. At the end, Cinderella forgives her stepsisters and matches them with two great lords of the court. Everyone gets a happy ending, even the mean ones.

cards.headline: The Grimms' fierce Cinderella
cards.body: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm's Children's and Household Tales (1812 to 1822) took most of its stories from oral sources, aiming to reproduce the teller's words and ways. Their Cinderella has no godmother. A hazel tree on her mother's grave and a white bird grant her wishes, and the slipper is golden. The stepsisters cut off a toe and a heel to squeeze into it. At the wedding, pigeons peck out their eyes.

mascot.line: People mix these up. Perrault polished old tales, the Grimms collected them, Andersen mostly invented his own.

cards.headline: Andersen wrote his own
cards.body: Hans Christian Andersen did something else again. All but a dozen of his 156 fairy tales are his own creations. From his first book of tales in 1835, he wrote in the idioms of the spoken language, breaking with literary tradition, and some of his tales are deeply pessimistic and end unhappily. Three tellers, three aims: polish an old tale, keep the folk voice, or invent a new one.

title: The Detective Story
objective: After this level you can use the fair-play rules of detective fiction, from Poe's Dupin to Sherlock Holmes, to spot a planted clue.
summary: Poe's Dupin (1841) set the detective pattern that Holmes and Watson (1887) followed. Fair play means every clue reaches you when it reaches the detective.

cards.headline: Sherlock Holmes on the first great detective: "very inferior".
cards.body: In A Study in Scarlet, Watson tells Holmes he reminds him of Poe's Dupin. Holmes is not flattered: "Dupin was a very inferior fellow." Rude, but revealing. Holmes had an ancestor, and the rules of his game were already set.

cards.headline: Poe invents the detective
cards.body: "The Murders in the Rue Morgue" by Edgar Allan Poe, the short-story craftsman of Level 71, published in April 1841, is called the first detective story. Its amateur detective, C. Auguste Dupin, solves a murder in a sealed room by reasoning from the clues, and his nameless friend tells the story. Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson, who narrates, first appeared in Arthur Conan Doyle's A Study in Scarlet (1887). Same pattern: a brilliant mind and a friend with a pen.

cards.headline: The rule of fair play
cards.body: Detective fiction grew a rule of fair play: the clues that lead to the solution should reach the reader at the same moment they reach the detective. In 1929 the writer Ronald Knox set out ten rules. Two of them: the criminal must be someone mentioned early in the story, and the detective must not find any clue that isn't shown to the reader at once. The mystery becomes a contest you could win.

mascot.line: Planted-clue test: could you have spotted it before the detective explained it? If so, the writer played fair.

objective: After this level you can explain how Jules Verne and H. G. Wells turned scientific what-ifs into fiction.
summary: Verne's From the Earth to the Moon (1865) treated space travel as engineering; Wells's Time Machine (1895) used the future to look at class in his own society.

cards.headline: In 1865, a novel aimed a giant cannon at the Moon.
cards.body: In Jules Verne's From the Earth to the Moon, members of the Baltimore Gun Club build an enormous cannon to shoot a "space-bullet" to the Moon from Florida. Absurd? Partly. But it asks the question at the heart of science fiction, which deals with the impact of science, real or imagined, on people.

cards.headline: Verne asks: can it be done?
cards.body: Verne's novel was the first fiction to treat space travel as a coherent engineering problem, recognizing, for example, that there could be no air. Yet he found no plausible way to land his cannon-fired passengers. In the sequel, Round the Moon (1870), they whiz past the Moon, cataloging craters. Verne's what-if was about the machine: how would you actually get there?

cards.headline: Wells asks: what would it do to us?
cards.body: H. G. Wells studied biology under T. H. Huxley and became a science teacher, but his what-ifs pointed at society. In The Time Machine (1895), the Time Traveller reaches the year 802,701 and finds the gentle Eloi above ground and the Morlocks below, who prey on them. The Eloi stand for the leisure class, the Morlocks for the working class. In The War of the Worlds (1898), invading Martians are killed by Earth's bacteria.

title: Dystopias
objective: After this level you can compare how Brave New World and Nineteen Eighty-Four imagine a society controlled by pleasure or by fear.
summary: Dystopias flip More's utopia into warnings. Huxley's Brave New World (1932) controls people by pleasure; Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949), by fear.

cards.headline: Two nightmares of the future: one keeps you scared, one keeps you happy.
cards.body: Aldous Huxley's Brave New World (1932) and George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four (1949) both imagine a society under total control. They disagree about how it's done. That disagreement is the key to reading them.

cards.headline: The opposite of utopia
cards.body: Thomas More coined the word utopia in his 1516 book of that name, a play on Greek meaning both "good place" and "no place". A dystopian novel flips it: a fictional society of dehumanization, fear and oppression. Dystopias often work as cautionary tales, taking trends of their own day and projecting them into a grim future. Britannica calls these two novels great didactic landmarks.

cards.headline: Huxley: control by pleasure
cards.body: In Brave New World, citizens are sorted as embryos into castes, from Alphas to Epsilons, and conditioned to fit their roles. Nobody has to be dragged anywhere. A pleasure-giving drug, soma, keeps everyone content and compliant. The prison is comfortable, and that's the horror.

cards.headline: Orwell: control by fear
cards.body: Orwell wrote Nineteen Eighty-Four as a warning against totalitarianism. The Party rules through the Thought Police and continual surveillance, and posters remind everyone that Big Brother is watching. Its invented language, Newspeak, is designed to limit free thought. Here obedience comes from fear.

title: Fantasy and Its Old Myths
objective: After this level you can trace how Tolkien built Middle-earth from Norse myth and Beowulf.
summary: Tolkien, an Oxford scholar of Old English, took dwarf names from the Poetic Edda and modeled Gandalf on Odin. Bilbo's stolen cup echoes Beowulf's dragon.

cards.headline: Tolkien's dwarves got their names from an Old Norse poem.
cards.body: Thorin, Durin, Bombur, Nori: the dwarves of Middle-earth sound made up. Yet their names match dwarves listed in the Völuspá, a poem of the Poetic Edda: the same poem that tells of Ragnarök in Level 12. Tolkien didn't only invent a world. He dug one up.

cards.headline: A professor of old words
cards.body: J. R. R. Tolkien taught at Oxford from 1925 to 1959, specializing in Old and Middle English, and gave a landmark 1936 lecture on Beowulf. The Hobbit followed in 1937, The Lord of the Rings in 1954 to 1955. In his letters he described a bigger ambition: to create a mythology for England. The raw material was on his desk.

cards.headline: A wizard in the shape of a god
cards.body: The names were only the start. Gandalf's likely model is Odin, the Norse king of the gods from Level 11, who in Norse poems travels among humans as a wandering wizard, coming and going with his own purposes. Sound familiar? That is Gandalf's whole job description.

cards.headline: One stolen cup
cards.body: In Beowulf (Level 47), a dragon is enraged when a man steals from its hoard; in J. Lesslie Hall's translation it misses its "gem-cup" and ravages the land with fire. In The Hobbit, Bilbo carries off a great two-handled cup from the sleeping Smaug, who wakes in fury. Copied? In a 1938 letter, Tolkien called Beowulf among his most valued sources, but said it wasn't consciously in his mind as he wrote: the theft arose naturally from the story.

title: Reading in Translation
objective: After this level you can weigh how two translations of the same passage can give a reader different pictures.
summary: Butler's prose Odyssey (1900) keeps Homer's repeated formulas; Pope's rhymed one (1725 to 1726) varies them. One Greek word, polytropos, gives several Odysseuses.

cards.headline: The same Greek sunrise, in two English versions.
cards.body: Book II of the Odyssey opens at dawn. Samuel Butler's translation: "Now when the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared". Alexander Pope's: "Now reddening from the dawn, the morning ray / Glow'd in the front of heaven". Same Greek. Two different mornings.

cards.headline: Prose or rhyme
cards.body: Butler's Odyssey, first published in 1900, is in plain English prose. He admitted the cost: much that is right in poetry, he wrote, is wrong in prose. Pope's Odyssey (1725 to 1726), a job he shared with William Broome and Elijah Fenton, is in rhyming heroic couplets of 10-syllable lines. Each choice gains something and gives something up.

cards.headline: One word, several heroes
cards.body: The first line calls Odysseus polytropos. The word can mean much-travelled or much-wandering, or, figuratively, turning many ways: versatile, wily. Butler writes "that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide", keeping both senses. Pope opens with "The man for wisdom's various arts renown'd", the clever man first, and brings in "Wandering from clime to clime" a few lines later. Neither is wrong. Each hands you a slightly different Odysseus.

cards.fact: Butler keeps Homer's repeated dawn. Pope varies it.
cards.context: In Butler, "the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn" comes back again and again, so you can watch the oral poet's building blocks at work. Pope renders the same dawn in varying words rather than one fixed phrase: Book II opens with "Now reddening from the dawn". Beautiful, but the repeated formula is harder to spot.

Pope: rhyming couplets, with the wording varied

title: Myths About Literature
objective: After this level you can debunk common myths, like Frankenstein being the monster's name or someone else writing Shakespeare's plays.
summary: Frankenstein is the maker, not the creature; Holmes never says "Elementary, my dear Watson"; and the Oxford theory of Shakespeare fails on dates.

mascot.line: This connects to Level 2. In this tree myth still means a sacred story; today's title just borrows the everyday word.

cards.headline: First, a word about this level's title.
cards.body: Level 2 said scholars use myth for a traditional sacred story, never for a falsehood. This title borrows the everyday sense instead. Scholars would call these misconceptions: popular beliefs about famous books that the books themselves don't back up. Let's test three.

cards.headline: Frankenstein is the doctor
cards.body: In Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818), which you met in Level 63, Frankenstein is Victor Frankenstein, a scientist who artificially creates a human being. The name is his, not his creation's. The Folger Shakespeare Library calls this one of the book's enduring confusions. Call the creature Frankenstein and, strictly, you've named the wrong character.

cards.headline: Holmes never said it
cards.body: "Elementary, my dear Watson" appears in none of Conan Doyle's stories. The nearest thing comes in The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes: "Excellent!" I cried. "Elementary," said he. Holmes does call his conclusions elementary now and then, and often says "my dear Watson". The full misquotation is first recorded in P. G. Wodehouse's Psmith, Journalist. Readers glued two real habits into a line he never spoke.

cards.headline: Who wrote Shakespeare? Shakespeare.
cards.body: For over 200 years after his death, nobody questioned that Shakespeare wrote his works. Doubts arose in the Victorian era, when Delia Bacon argued for a circle of writers including Francis Bacon and Walter Raleigh, and in 1920 J. Thomas Looney proposed Edward de Vere, earl of Oxford. Scholars overwhelmingly reject these candidates. Oxford died in 1604, yet by standard dating more than a dozen plays were written after that. And in the First Folio (1623), Ben Jonson hailed him as the "Sweet Swan of Avon", tying the writer to Stratford.

title: Why a Classic Matters
objective: After this level you can use the whole tree to place a classic you pick up in its tradition and explain why it matters.
summary: Twain joked that a classic is praised, not read. Calvino said it never finishes saying what it has to say. Three questions place any classic: try Gilgamesh.

cards.headline: Mark Twain on classics: praised, not read.
cards.body: In Following the Equator (1897), Twain offered a definition: "Classic." A book which people praise and don't read. It's a good joke, and sometimes true. This level is about proving it wrong: what makes a classic worth reading, and how to place one you pick up.

cards.headline: A book that isn't finished with you
cards.body: The Italian novelist Italo Calvino gave a better answer in his essay "Why Read the Classics?". A classic, he suggested, never runs out of things to say. It also reaches you carrying traces of the readings before yours, and of the marks it has left on languages and customs. So a classic isn't just old. It is still talking, and it brings its history with it.

cards.headline: Three questions for any classic
cards.body: Calvino's traces suggest three questions, and this tree has given you tools for each. Where does it come from? The Grimms, for example, took most of their tales from oral sources. How does it work? A detective story plays fair and shows you each clue as the detective finds it. What have others taken from it? Ovid gave scores of Greek legends the form later generations knew, and Beowulf became one of Tolkien's most valued sources.

cards.fact: Try the three questions on Gilgamesh.
cards.context: Where from? Mesopotamia: its fullest text survives on 12 clay tablets found at Nineveh. How does it work? It's an epic, a long narrative poem about heroic deeds. What does it still say? A king who helps kill Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven still loses the plant of youth to a serpent and goes home mortal. Calvino's test, passed by one of the oldest stories we have.
